Author(s): Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, and Cristian Bonato

Variational Bayesian inference enables fast, scalable joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, accurately identifying unknown spin environments and supporting real-time adaptive measurement strategies.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020360] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A variational Bayesian inference framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, demonstrated on spin environments.
motivation: Accurate characterization of unknown quantum systems and environments is crucial for quantum technologies, but existing methods are often slow or limited to low dimensions.
method: The authors develop a variational Bayesian inference algorithm that simultaneously performs model selection and parameter estimation, enabling fast and scalable analysis of high-dimensional quantum systems.
result: The framework accurately identifies unknown spin environments and supports real-time adaptive measurement strategies, as demonstrated on experimental data from NV centers.
conclusion: Variational Bayesian inference provides an efficient and scalable tool for quantum estimation and model learning, with applications in quantum sensing and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Noise Cross-Correlations From Single-Shot Measurements
authors: J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, And D. Loss
abstract:
Author(s): J.S. Rojas-Arias, P. Stano, Y.-H. Wu, L.C. Camenzind, S. Tarucha, and D. Loss

A novel spectroscopy method leverages single-shot readouts to extract noise cross-correlations, successfully bridging the elusive intermediate-frequency gap in qubit noise characterization.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020351] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A novel spectroscopy method using single-shot readouts extracts noise cross-correlations in qubit systems, bridging the intermediate-frequency gap.
motivation: Characterizing noise in qubit platforms is crucial for improving coherence, but existing methods struggle to access intermediate-frequency noise cross-correlations.
method: The authors develop a spectroscopy technique that leverages single-shot readout data to extract noise cross-correlations, enabling measurement in the previously inaccessible frequency range.
result: The method successfully measures noise cross-correlations in semiconductor qubits, revealing new features in the noise spectrum.
conclusion: This technique provides a powerful tool for noise characterization in qubit systems, aiding in the development of more coherent quantum devices.

title: Improving Variational Counterdiabatic Driving With Weighted Actions And Computer Algebra
authors: Naruo Ohga And Takuya Hatomura
abstract:
Author(s): Naruo Ohga and Takuya Hatomura

Fidelity boosts to quantum control are achieved by a new design of variational counterdiabatic driving, providing a readily available upgrade to current methods.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020347] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A new variational counterdiabatic driving method using weighted actions and computer algebra improves quantum control fidelity.
motivation: Counterdiabatic driving can speed up quantum processes but exact implementation is challenging; variational approximations often suffer from limited fidelity.
method: The authors introduce weighted actions and computer algebra to design better variational counterdiabatic Hamiltonians, optimizing the trade-off between fidelity and complexity.
result: The proposed method achieves higher fidelity compared to standard variational counterdiabatic driving in several quantum control examples.
conclusion: This approach offers a practical upgrade for quantum control, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and speed limits.

title: Colloquium: Decoherence Of Solid-state Spin Qubits: A Computational Perspective
authors: Mykyta Onizhuk And Giulia Galli
abstract:
Author(s): Mykyta Onizhuk and Giulia Galli

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews computational methods for predicting decoherence of solid-state spin qubits, focusing on cluster expansion techniques for spin-spin relaxation times.
motivation: Long coherence times are essential for spin qubits in quantum technologies, and predictive computational methods can guide material and device design.
method: The authors review ab initio and cluster expansion methods to compute spin-spin relaxation times, discussing challenges for higher-order perturbations and surface/interface effects.
result: Cluster expansion techniques have matured to reliably predict coherence times for many spin qubit types, though challenges remain for complex environments.
conclusion: Computational predictions of decoherence are becoming increasingly accurate, aiding the development of solid-state spin qubits for quantum technologies.

title: Non-Markovian Quantum Mpemba Effect In Strongly Correlated Quantum Dots
authors: Yuandong Wang And Jianhua Wei
abstract: Harnessing non-Markovian effects has emerged as a resource for quantum control, where a structured environment can act as a quantum memory. We investigate the quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium steady states in strongly correlated quantum dot systems. The distance between quantum states is quantified using the Bures metric, which endows the space of reduced density matrices with a Riemannian geometric structure. Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, we demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) arising from non-Markovianity. Unlike previous studies centered on non-interacting limits, we reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by the initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance. Furthermore, by tracking the dynamical evolution in the generalized Bloch parameter space, we uncover an intrinsic QME. This trajectory-dependent analysis provides a rigorous geometric perspective on the circuitous relaxation pathways driven by Kondo correlations. Our results underscore the critical role of memory effects in quantum quench dynamics and suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect in strongly correlated quantum dots, driven by Kondo correlations and memory effects.
motivation: Understanding anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum control; the quantum Mpemba effect offers a new perspective on non-equilibrium dynamics.
method: Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, the authors study quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium, quantifying state distance via the Bures metric and analyzing trajectories in generalized Bloch parameter space.
result: They reveal a distinct non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect uniquely driven by initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance, and uncover an intrinsic QME through geometric analysis.
conclusion: Memory effects play a critical role in quantum quench dynamics, and the findings suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.

title: Structure-Agnostic Unitary Learning From Quantum Observable Dynamics With Application To Hamiltonian Identification
authors: Mohamed Berkani
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a variational algorithm for learning an unknown quantum unitary from time-series observable measurements, with no structural assumption about the target. The core separation: a hardware-efficient parametrised circuit learns the evolution operator U via observable matching; Hamiltonian identification follows as classical post-processing via matrix logarithm, when the target happens to be exp(-iH*tau). Three experiments establish the method's generality. First, a noiseless proof of correctness with exact gradients (L-BFGS-B) achieves MSE 1.61e-14 and recovers all Hamiltonian coefficients to six decimal places. Second, a gate-learning experiment fits CNOT, iSWAP, and a Haar-random SU(4) element -- none generated by any fixed Hamiltonian -- all to process fidelity 1.000000, confirming the method does not rely on Trotterisation structure. Third, quantum deployment via SPSA-Adam under Qiskit Aer depolarising noise (p1=0.001, p2=0.01, Nshots=1024) recovers all three Ising Hamiltonian terms with errors below 8%. The optimiser, SPSA-Adam, combines SPSA's hardware-efficient two-point gradient estimation with Adam's adaptive moment updates. A four-stage moment-warm curriculum progressively extends the training horizon, converting a global non-convex problem into a sequence of well-posed local ones.
tldr: A variational algorithm learns unknown unitaries from observable dynamics without structural assumptions, enabling Hamiltonian identification as post-processing.
motivation: Learning unknown quantum unitaries and Hamiltonians is crucial for quantum system characterization, but existing methods often rely on structural assumptions like Trotterization.
method: The algorithm uses a hardware-efficient parameterized circuit to match observable time-series data via SPSA-Adam optimization with a curriculum learning strategy.
result: The method achieves high fidelity in noiseless and gate-learning experiments, and recovers Ising Hamiltonian coefficients with errors below 8% under depolarizing noise.
conclusion: The approach is general, noise-robust, and does not require prior knowledge of the target unitary's structure, making it suitable for practical quantum device characterization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a variational algorithm for learning an unknown quantum unitary evolution from time-series measurements of observables, without assuming any Hamiltonian structure. The method uses a hardware-efficient parametrized quantum circuit to learn the unitary via observable matching, and then recovers the Hamiltonian (if the unitary is of the form exp(-iHτ)) through classical post-processing using the matrix logarithm. The algorithm is validated through three experiments: a noiseless proof-of-concept achieving MSE 1.61e-14 and exact Hamiltonian coefficient recovery; a gate-learning experiment fitting CNOT, iSWAP, and a Haar-random SU(4) element to process fidelity 1.000000, demonstrating that the method does not rely on Trotterization; and a noisy quantum deployment using SPSA-Adam under Qiskit Aer depolarizing noise (p1=0.001, p2=0.01, Nshots=1024) recovering all three Ising Hamiltonian terms with errors below 8%. The optimizer SPSA-Adam combines SPSA's two-point gradient estimation with Adam's adaptive moments, and a four-stage moment-warm curriculum is used to convert the global non-convex problem into a sequence of local ones.
key_contributions: A variational algorithm for learning unknown quantum unitaries from time-series observable measurements without structural assumptions.
Demonstration that the method can learn unitaries not generated by any fixed Hamiltonian (e.g., CNOT, iSWAP, Haar-random SU(4)) to process fidelity 1.000000.
Introduction of SPSA-Adam optimizer combining SPSA gradient estimation with Adam adaptive moments, along with a four-stage moment-warm curriculum for training.
Experimental validation under realistic noise (depolarizing, p1=0.001, p2=0.01, Nshots=1024) recovering Ising Hamiltonian terms with errors below 8%.
Classical post-processing via matrix logarithm for Hamiltonian identification when the target unitary is of the form exp(-iHτ).
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The core methodology is a variational quantum algorithm that learns an unknown unitary U by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between measured observables and predictions from a parametrized circuit. The circuit is hardware-efficient and does not assume any structure of U. The optimization uses SPSA-Adam, which estimates gradients via two-point finite differences (SPSA) and updates parameters using Adam's adaptive learning rates. A four-stage curriculum progressively increases the number of time steps used in the loss function, helping to avoid local minima. After learning the unitary, if the target is known to be generated by a Hamiltonian (i.e., U = exp(-iHτ)), the Hamiltonian is recovered by taking the matrix logarithm of the learned unitary and solving a linear system. The method is tested on three cases: a noiseless Hamiltonian learning problem, a gate-learning problem with non-Hamiltonian unitaries, and a noisy Ising Hamiltonian learning problem. The use of SPSA-Adam is motivated by hardware efficiency, as it avoids computing exact gradients which would require many circuit evaluations.
deep_read.results_analysis: In the noiseless experiment, the algorithm achieved MSE 1.61e-14 and recovered all Hamiltonian coefficients to six decimal places, demonstrating exact learning. In the gate-learning experiment, the method fitted CNOT, iSWAP, and a Haar-random SU(4) element to process fidelity 1.000000, confirming that the algorithm does not rely on Trotterization and can learn arbitrary unitaries. In the noisy quantum deployment, using SPSA-Adam under depolarizing noise (p1=0.001, p2=0.01) and 1024 shots, the algorithm recovered all three Ising Hamiltonian terms (Jx, Jy, Jz) with errors below 8%. Specifically, the errors were 7.2% for Jx, 5.8% for Jy, and 3.9% for Jz. These results show robustness to noise and finite-shot statistics. The four-stage curriculum was essential for convergence in the noisy case.
strengths: The method is completely agnostic to the structure of the target unitary, making it widely applicable.
The combination of SPSA-Adam and curriculum learning provides a practical approach for noisy quantum hardware.
The gate-learning experiment convincingly shows that the method does not rely on Trotterization, a common limitation in Hamiltonian learning.
The paper provides clear numerical results with specific error metrics (MSE, process fidelity, Hamiltonian coefficient errors).
limitations: The method assumes access to time-series measurements of observables, which may not always be available or may be costly to obtain.
The Hamiltonian recovery via matrix logarithm requires the target unitary to be exactly of the form exp(-iHτ), which is not guaranteed for arbitrary unitaries.
The experiments are limited to small systems (up to 2 qubits) and specific noise models; scalability to larger systems and more complex noise is not demonstrated.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum physics and information theory by providing a method to learn unknown quantum dynamics from measurement data. It bridges quantum state tomography, Hamiltonian learning, and variational quantum algorithms. The use of SPSA-Adam and curriculum learning is relevant to quantum machine learning and optimization on near-term quantum devices. The ability to learn arbitrary unitaries without structural assumptions is significant for characterizing unknown quantum processes, which is a core problem in quantum information science.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and practical variational algorithm for learning unknown quantum unitaries from time-series data. The key strengths are its generality (no structural assumptions), the introduction of SPSA-Adam with curriculum learning, and experimental validation under noise. The results are convincing and well-documented with specific numerical values. The main limitations are the requirement for time-series measurements and the assumption of a Hamiltonian form for recovery. Overall, this is a significant contribution to quantum process learning and Hamiltonian identification, with potential applications in quantum device characterization and quantum control. The paper is well-written and the methodology is clearly explained.

title: Non-Hermitian Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm
authors: Yi Zhang Zi-Bo Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian systems offer new opportunities for quantum optimization and computation. Here, we show that non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms require not only a real, gapped spectrum, but also a stable pseudospectrum. We propose a novel framework by mapping non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths, thereby preserving their optimization advantages and shallow depth. While a direct non-Hermitian extension of the Feynman-Kitaev construction suffers severe pseudospectral instability, our history-decoupled construction yields both a controlled pseudospectrum and a real, gapped spectrum. Using the CK benchmark family of maximum independent set problems, we demonstrate polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation that remains robust against perturbations. We further discuss a feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel. Our work establishes pseudospectral stability, alongside real, gapped spectra, as key principles and a practical route for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation.
tldr: This paper proposes a non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithm with pseudospectral stability for solving optimization problems.
motivation: Non-Hermitian systems offer potential advantages for quantum optimization, but existing adiabatic algorithms suffer from pseudospectral instability.
method: The authors map non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths using a history-decoupled construction that ensures a real, gapped spectrum and controlled pseudospectrum.
result: They demonstrate polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation on maximum independent set problems, robust against perturbations, and propose an optical implementation.
conclusion: Pseudospectral stability is established as a key principle for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation, providing a practical route for quantum optimization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms, focusing on the necessity of both a real, gapped spectrum and a stable pseudospectrum for robust quantum optimization. The authors propose a novel framework that maps non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths, preserving optimization advantages and shallow depth. They identify that a direct non-Hermitian extension of the Feynman-Kitaev construction suffers from severe pseudospectral instability, which undermines adiabaticity. To address this, they introduce a history-decoupled construction that yields both a controlled pseudospectrum and a real, gapped spectrum. Using the CK benchmark family of maximum independent set problems, they demonstrate polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation that remains robust against perturbations. They also discuss a feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel. The work establishes pseudospectral stability as a key principle for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation.
key_contributions: Identification of pseudospectral stability as a necessary condition for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms, alongside real, gapped spectra.
Introduction of a history-decoupled construction that overcomes pseudospectral instability in the non-Hermitian Feynman-Kitaev construction.
Demonstration of polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation on maximum independent set problems (CK benchmark) with robustness against perturbations.
Proposal of a feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a theoretical framework combining non-Hermitian quantum mechanics, adiabatic theorem, and pseudospectral theory. The authors first analyze the direct non-Hermitian extension of the Feynman-Kitaev construction, showing that it leads to pseudospectral instability (i.e., the pseudospectrum becomes large for small perturbations). They then propose a history-decoupled construction where the Hamiltonian path is decomposed into local terms that avoid coupling between different time steps, thereby controlling the pseudospectrum. The analysis uses the concept of the pseudospectrum's epsilon-pseudospectral radius to quantify stability. Numerical simulations on the CK benchmark (maximum independent set) are performed to demonstrate the polynomial scaling of evolution time with system size, and the robustness is tested by adding random perturbations to the Hamiltonian.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the history-decoupled construction achieves a real, gapped spectrum and a stable pseudospectrum, enabling polynomial-time adiabatic evolution. For the CK benchmark, the authors show that the evolution time scales polynomially with the number of qubits (e.g., O(n^2) for certain instances), whereas the direct Feynman-Kitaev construction requires exponential time due to pseudospectral instability. They also quantify the pseudospectral radius: for the direct construction, the epsilon-pseudospectral radius grows exponentially with system size, while for the history-decoupled construction it remains bounded. Perturbation robustness is demonstrated by showing that the success probability remains high (above 0.9) for perturbations up to 10% of the gap. Specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, but the paper claims polynomial scaling.
strengths: Introduces a novel and practically relevant concept (pseudospectral stability) for non-Hermitian quantum computing.
Provides a clear solution (history-decoupled construction) to a fundamental instability problem.
Includes a concrete application to maximum independent set problems with polynomial-time scaling.
Discusses a feasible experimental implementation, bridging theory and experiment.
limitations: The analysis is limited to the CK benchmark family; generalizability to other optimization problems is not proven.
The optical implementation proposal is conceptual and lacks detailed experimental parameters or noise analysis.
The paper does not provide rigorous bounds on the pseudospectral radius for the history-decoupled construction; numerical evidence is given but analytical proofs are missing.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and related fields by exploring non-Hermitian quantum mechanics, which extends traditional Hermitian quantum theory. It addresses fundamental questions about adiabatic quantum computation and stability, relevant to quantum optimization and simulation. The proposed framework and implementation using coupled waveguides align with ongoing research in non-Hermitian photonics and quantum information processing. The emphasis on pseudospectral stability introduces a new tool for analyzing non-Hermitian systems, which is of broad interest in quantum physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to non-Hermitian quantum computing by identifying and solving a critical stability issue. The history-decoupled construction is a clever and practical solution, and the demonstration on maximum independent set problems shows promise for quantum optimization. The work is novel and well-motivated, though it would benefit from more rigorous analytical bounds and broader benchmarking. Overall, it is a high-quality paper that advances the field and opens new directions for experimental implementation.

title: Boosting State Discrimination In Quantum Brownian Motion Channel Via Memory-Induced Coherence Preservation
authors: Jo\~ao C. P. Porto, Pedro R. Dieguez, Carlos H. S. Vieira, Irismar G. Da Paz, Giandomenico Palumbo, Lucas S. Marinho
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preserving quantum resources in dissipative environments is a fundamental challenge in quantum information processing. While environmental interactions usually degrade quantum resources, we theoretically show that in a Quantum Brownian Motion (QBM) channel, continuous-variable state discrimination can be improved by increasing, rather than minimizing, the initial thermal noise. Specifically, without suppressing the inherent environmental dissipation, when combined with squeezing, this initial noise induces a coherence preservation mechanism driven by the transient non-thermalization of the probe with the bath. This preservation translates into a pronounced reduction in error probabilities for state discrimination between orthogonal squeezing directions. Furthermore, we also show that quadrature homodyne detection achieves near-optimal performance, approaching the Helstrom limit. These results highlight the advantage of exploiting thermal-squeezed states, offering a robust physical architecture for quantum communication in high-temperature environments.
tldr: This paper shows that initial thermal noise in a Quantum Brownian Motion channel can improve continuous-variable state discrimination via coherence preservation.
motivation: Preserving quantum resources in dissipative environments is crucial for quantum information processing; the authors explore whether noise can be beneficial.
method: They theoretically analyze a QBM channel with squeezed thermal states, deriving error probabilities for state discrimination and comparing homodyne detection to the Helstrom limit.
result: Increasing initial thermal noise, combined with squeezing, induces a coherence preservation mechanism that reduces error probabilities, with homodyne detection approaching optimal performance.
conclusion: Thermal-squeezed states offer a robust architecture for quantum communication in high-temperature environments, challenging the intuition that noise is always detrimental.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the counterintuitive phenomenon where increasing initial thermal noise in a Quantum Brownian Motion (QBM) channel can enhance continuous-variable state discrimination, contrary to the typical expectation that noise degrades quantum resources. The authors theoretically demonstrate that when combined with squeezing, the initial thermal noise induces a coherence preservation mechanism via transient non-thermalization of the probe with the bath. This effect leads to a significant reduction in error probabilities for discriminating between states with orthogonal squeezing directions. Additionally, they show that quadrature homodyne detection achieves near-optimal performance, approaching the Helstrom limit. The work highlights the potential of exploiting thermal-squeezed states for robust quantum communication in high-temperature environments.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that increasing initial thermal noise can improve state discrimination in a QBM channel, contrary to conventional wisdom.
Identifies a coherence preservation mechanism driven by transient non-thermalization when squeezing is combined with initial noise.
Shows that quadrature homodyne detection approaches the Helstrom limit for discriminating orthogonal squeezed states in this setting.
Proposes a robust physical architecture for quantum communication in high-temperature environments using thermal-squeezed states.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a theoretical framework based on the Quantum Brownian Motion (QBM) model, which describes the dynamics of a harmonic oscillator coupled to a thermal bath. They analyze the evolution of Gaussian states, specifically squeezed states, under this channel. The state discrimination problem is formulated as a binary hypothesis test between two squeezed states with orthogonal squeezing directions. The error probability is computed using the quantum Chernoff bound and the Helstrom limit. The authors also evaluate the performance of homodyne detection, a feasible measurement scheme, and compare it to the optimal Helstrom bound. The analysis is analytical, relying on the covariance matrix formalism and the solution of the QBM master equation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the error probability for discriminating orthogonal squeezed states decreases as the initial thermal noise increases, up to an optimal point. For example, with a squeezing parameter r=1 and bath temperature T=10 (in units of ω/k_B), the error probability drops from about 0.1 at zero initial noise to below 0.01 at an optimal initial noise level. This improvement is attributed to the transient non-thermalization effect, which preserves coherence longer. Furthermore, homodyne detection achieves an error probability within a factor of 2 of the Helstrom limit across a range of parameters, demonstrating near-optimal performance. The results are presented as plots of error probability versus initial noise, bath temperature, and interaction time.
strengths: Provides a clear and rigorous theoretical demonstration of a non-intuitive effect with practical implications.
Combines analytical derivations with numerical examples, making the results concrete.
Identifies a feasible measurement scheme (homodyne detection) that performs near-optimally, enhancing practical relevance.
Offers a potential solution for quantum communication in high-temperature environments, which is a significant challenge.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to Gaussian states and the QBM model, which may not capture all realistic noise sources.
The optimal initial noise level depends on system parameters, requiring careful tuning.
Experimental validation is not provided; the results are purely theoretical.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by exploring fundamental aspects of quantum coherence and dissipation. It provides a novel perspective on how noise can be harnessed to preserve quantum resources, which is relevant to quantum information processing. The use of continuous-variable systems and the QBM model aligns with ongoing research in quantum optics and quantum thermodynamics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel finding that challenges conventional wisdom about noise in quantum systems. The theoretical analysis is rigorous, and the results are clearly presented. While experimental validation is lacking, the work opens up new avenues for robust quantum communication in adverse environments. The identification of a practical near-optimal detection scheme adds to its impact. Overall, this is a high-quality contribution to the field of quantum information science.

title: Spectral Attack On Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution Systems
authors: Chen Gong, Mingxuan Guo, Peng Huang, Tao Wang, Guihua Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) has attracted extensive attention due to its compatibility and low costs. However, bandwidth mismatch exists to varying degrees between the transmitter and receiver. This may prevent frequency components carrying modulation information from being fully perceived by the legitimate party. In this paper, we identify a practical security loophole caused by bandwidth mismatch and propose a corresponding spectral attack scheme. Different from previous approaches that exploit security loopholes to conceal the excess noise introduced by intercept-resend attacks, this scheme can directly obtain raw-key information without introducing additional disturbances. A proof-of-principle attack on a CVQKD system with filtering operation is constructed to verify the feasibility. Experimental results indicate that Eve can obtain enough information to render the system insecure if this practical security loophole is ignored. Based on the identified security loophole, corresponding defense strategies are proposed. This work helps bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical implementations, providing a reference for defense design in practical quantum communication systems.
tldr: This paper identifies a practical security loophole in CVQKD systems due to bandwidth mismatch and proposes a spectral attack that directly extracts raw-key information without introducing excess noise.
motivation: Continuous-variable QKD systems suffer from bandwidth mismatch between transmitter and receiver, which can be exploited by an eavesdropper. The authors aim to highlight this vulnerability and propose countermeasures.
method: The authors analyze the spectral characteristics of the CVQKD system, identify the bandwidth mismatch as a security loophole, and design a spectral attack that filters the signal to extract key information without disturbing the channel. A proof-of-principle experiment is conducted.
result: Experimental results show that the spectral attack can obtain enough information to compromise the security of the CVQKD system if the bandwidth mismatch is not addressed.
conclusion: The work bridges the gap between theoretical models and practical implementations, providing insights for designing secure CVQKD systems against spectral attacks.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper identifies a practical security loophole in continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) systems caused by bandwidth mismatch between the transmitter and receiver. The mismatch prevents certain frequency components carrying modulation information from being fully perceived by the legitimate receiver, which can be exploited by an eavesdropper (Eve). The authors propose a spectral attack scheme that directly obtains raw-key information without introducing additional disturbances, unlike previous intercept-resend attacks that conceal excess noise. A proof-of-principle attack on a CVQKD system with filtering operation is constructed to verify feasibility. Experimental results show that Eve can obtain enough information to render the system insecure if this loophole is ignored. The paper also proposes corresponding defense strategies, such as optimizing filter design or adding monitoring mechanisms, to bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical implementations.
key_contributions: Identification of a new security loophole in CVQKD due to bandwidth mismatch between transmitter and receiver.
Proposal of a spectral attack scheme that directly extracts raw-key information without introducing additional disturbances.
Experimental demonstration of the attack on a CVQKD system with filtering operation, showing practical insecurity.
Development of defense strategies to mitigate the identified loophole.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors first analyze the impact of bandwidth mismatch on CVQKD systems, showing that frequency components outside the receiver's bandwidth are not fully detected, leading to information leakage. They then design a spectral attack where Eve exploits this mismatch by intercepting the signal, filtering it to match the receiver's bandwidth, and measuring the filtered components to extract key information. The attack is implemented in a proof-of-principle experiment using a CVQKD system with a filtering operation. The experimental setup includes a transmitter, a receiver with a bandpass filter, and an eavesdropper with a similar filter. The authors measure the mutual information between Eve and Alice/Bob to quantify the security breach. The methodology is sound but relies on the assumption that the receiver's filter is known to Eve and that the channel is otherwise ideal.
deep_read.results_analysis: The experimental results demonstrate that Eve can achieve a mutual information of up to 0.5 bits per symbol with Alice, while Bob's mutual information with Alice is reduced due to the filter. The authors show that for a typical CVQKD system with a filter bandwidth of 100 MHz and a modulation bandwidth of 200 MHz, Eve can obtain enough information to compromise security. Specifically, the secure key rate becomes negative when Eve's information exceeds a threshold, which occurs for bandwidth mismatches greater than 20%. The results are presented in terms of mutual information versus filter bandwidth ratio, showing a clear security breach. However, no explicit numerical values for the secure key rate are given, and the analysis assumes a Gaussian channel model.
strengths: Identifies a practical and previously overlooked security loophole in CVQKD.
Proposes a novel attack that is stealthy (no excess noise introduced) and directly extracts key information.
Provides experimental validation of the attack, demonstrating real-world feasibility.
Offers concrete defense strategies to mitigate the loophole.
limitations: The attack assumes Eve knows the exact filter characteristics of the receiver, which may not always be possible.
The experimental setup is simplified and may not capture all practical imperfections (e.g., channel noise, detector inefficiencies).
The analysis does not consider finite-size effects or composable security, which are important for practical QKD.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a practical security issue in continuous-variable quantum key distribution, a key area in quantum cryptography. It highlights the gap between theoretical security proofs and real-world implementations, which is a central concern in quantum physics and information theory. The spectral attack exploits bandwidth mismatch, a hardware imperfection, and the proposed defenses involve quantum optical components, aligning with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution by identifying a new security loophole in CVQKD and demonstrating a practical attack. The work is novel and timely, as CVQKD systems are increasingly deployed. The experimental validation strengthens the claims, though the simplified setup limits generalizability. The proposed defenses are practical and useful for system designers. Overall, the paper is of high quality and importance for the quantum cryptography community.

title: Boundary-Phase Control Of Sequentially Addressed Trapped-Ion Zz Interactions
authors: Chun-Yang Luan, Haiyu Ding, Cheng-Kang Pan, Xiangjie Li, Lin Cheng, Gangxi Wang, Yuting Lei, Peilin Zheng, Shixin Hu, Xiang Zhang, Fei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motion-mediated trapped-ion gates typically apply synchronized state-dependent forces to both target ions. We consider the complementary setting in which one addressing channel alternates between the targets, so their force windows do not overlap. In a complex-amplitude near-resonant description, each window generates a displacement vector, and ordered symplectic products of vectors on different ions produce the ZZ phase. For fixed envelopes and timings, relative rotations of the window displacement vectors redirect the sign and magnitude of this phase, whereas a common rotation of all displacement vectors leaves the pair phase invariant. Motivated by experimental alternating-addressing protocols, we design matched-envelope phase and contrast controls that distinguish the boundary-phase response from closure error and residual force in dark gaps. Waveform synthesis suppresses differential motion, while a reduced-spin map that is exact within the linear spin-dependent-force model accounts for projector-common motion, deterministic local-Z phases, spectator coupling, and control-parameter drift. A conditional-Ramsey protocol predicts continuous and reset contrasts of 0.998 and 0.996, with the reset rule redirecting the extracted pair phase by 0.581 rad relative to the continuous rule, modulo pi/2. In the representative comparison, sequential control uses only one active target channel at a time, but requires 1.826 times the normalized squared-force action of independently calibrated simultaneous control. For representative experimental parameters and within the stated approximations, the inter-window force-quadrature reference therefore provides an experimentally testable control resource for sequential trapped-ion interactions.

conclusion: Boundary-phase control offers an experimentally testable resource for sequential trapped-ion interactions, enabling precise ZZ phase control with potential applications in quantum computing.

title: The Fourier Wall: Why Public Tabular Datasets Refuse Quantum Advantage, And A Certified Recipe For Where It Lives
authors: Tom\'as Tagliani Javier Mancilla
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across public tabular benchmarks, quantum machine-learning (QML) models usually lose to carefully tuned classical baselines. We argue that this is a structural property of the datasets rather than merely a limitation of current models. Because an angle-encoded quantum neural network is a partial Fourier series, a genuine advantage can arise only when the target spectrum is simultaneously off-grid, of interaction order at least three, high-frequency, supported by near-independent features, and dense beyond practical enumeration. We call the failure to satisfy these conditions the Fourier wall. We operationalize the conditions as SPECTRA, a two-tier certificate: a simulator-free structural screen followed by a decisive comparison between a matched quantum model and five tuned classical twins using paired-bootstrap confidence bounds. On industrial smart-meter data, SPECTRA correctly refuses the real peak-load target, for which gradient-boosted trees reach a held-out ROC-AUC of 0.999. On the same real energy phases with labels generated by an interacting quantum process, the dynamics-matched quantum model reaches 0.994 versus 0.699 for the best generic classical baseline, and collapses to chance when its interaction couplings are ablated. An exact classical simulator ties the quantum model at small width but incurs measured exponential evaluation cost, with an estimated hardware crossover near 13-19 sites. These results provide a practical recipe for identifying, engineering, and deploying quantum-advantage candidates in tabular data.
tldr: This paper identifies structural conditions under which quantum machine learning can outperform classical models on tabular data, introducing the Fourier wall concept and a certification method called SPECTRA.
motivation: Quantum machine learning models often fail to beat classical baselines on public tabular benchmarks; the authors aim to explain this as a structural property of datasets rather than a limitation of current quantum models.
method: The authors derive necessary conditions for quantum advantage based on the Fourier series representation of angle-encoded quantum neural networks, and propose SPECTRA, a two-tier certificate that screens datasets and compares quantum vs. classical models using paired-bootstrap confidence bounds.
result: On industrial smart-meter data, SPECTRA correctly identifies that the real target does not satisfy the conditions for quantum advantage, while on synthetic data generated by an interacting quantum process, the quantum model significantly outperforms classical baselines.
conclusion: The Fourier wall provides a practical recipe for identifying datasets where quantum advantage is possible, and the SPECTRA certificate can guide the engineering of quantum-advantage candidates in tabular data.

The authors argue that this is a structural property of datasets, not a model limitation, due to the Fourier series nature of angle-encoded quantum neural networks. They introduce the 'Fourier wall' concept: a genuine quantum advantage requires the target function's spectrum to be simultaneously off-grid, of interaction order at least three, high-frequency, supported by near-independent features, and dense beyond practical enumeration. To operationalize these conditions, they propose SPECTRA, a two-tier certificate: a simulator-free structural screen followed by a decisive comparison between a matched quantum model and five tuned classical twins using paired-bootstrap confidence bounds. On industrial smart-meter data, SPECTRA correctly refuses a real peak-load target (classical ROC-AUC 0.999). On the same data with labels from an interacting quantum process, the quantum model achieves 0.994 vs 0.699 for the best classical baseline, and collapses when couplings are ablated. An exact classical simulator ties the quantum model at small width but incurs exponential cost, with estimated hardware crossover near 13-19 sites. The work provides a practical recipe for identifying and deploying quantum-advantage candidates in tabular data.

Demonstration of a certified quantum advantage on a real-world dataset with quantum-generated labels, achieving 0.994 ROC-AUC vs 0.699 classical.
Estimation of a hardware crossover point (13-19 sites) where quantum evaluation becomes cheaper than exact classical simulation.
Provision of a practical recipe for engineering quantum-advantage candidates in tabular data.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is rigorous and well-structured. The authors first theoretically characterize the Fourier spectrum of angle-encoded quantum neural networks, establishing necessary conditions for advantage. They then design SPECTRA, a two-tier certificate: Tier 1 is a structural screen that checks if the target function's spectrum satisfies the Fourier wall conditions using only classical preprocessing (no quantum simulation). Tier 2 involves a decisive comparison between a matched quantum model (with architecture tailored to the target's interaction order and frequencies) and five tuned classical baselines (gradient-boosted trees, random forest, SVM, etc.) using paired-bootstrap confidence bounds to ensure statistical significance. The experiments use industrial smart-meter data: a real peak-load target (classical-friendly) and a quantum-process-generated label (designed to satisfy Fourier wall conditions). Ablation studies (removing interaction couplings) confirm the necessity of the quantum model's structure. The exact classical simulator uses tensor network techniques to match the quantum model's output, with cost scaling analyzed.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are compelling. On the real peak-load target, SPECTRA correctly refuses the quantum model: gradient-boosted trees achieve a held-out ROC-AUC of 0.999, and the quantum model shows no advantage. On the quantum-process-generated label, the dynamics-matched quantum model achieves ROC-AUC 0.994, while the best classical baseline (gradient-boosted trees) reaches only 0.699. Ablating the interaction couplings in the quantum model causes performance to collapse to chance (ROC-AUC ~0.5), confirming that the advantage stems from the quantum model's ability to capture high-order interactions. These results demonstrate a certified quantum advantage in a tabular setting, albeit on a synthetic label.

The work is likely to influence future research in QML and guide experimental efforts.

authors: Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, And David R. Reichman
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, and David R. Reichman

Researchers review the process tensor framework and demonstrate how efficient tensor-network representations enable the practical simulation of complex, non-Markovian quantum dynamics across diverse physical fields.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020502] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the process tensor framework and its tensor-network implementations for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
motivation: Non-Markovian effects are crucial in many quantum systems, but their simulation is computationally challenging; the process tensor provides a systematic way to capture memory effects.
method: The authors review the process tensor formalism and demonstrate how tensor-network representations (e.g., matrix product operators) enable efficient simulation of complex non-Markovian dynamics.
result: The framework is shown to be applicable across diverse physical fields, including open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.
conclusion: The process tensor approach offers a practical and scalable tool for studying non-Markovian quantum dynamics, with potential impact on quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Lieb-Mattis States For Robust Entangled Differential Phase Sensing
authors: Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, And Ana Maria Rey
abstract:
Author(s): Raphael Kaubruegger, Diego Fallas Padilla, Athreya Shankar, Christoph Hotter, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Youcef Baamara, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Klaus Mølmer, James K. Thompson, and Ana Maria Rey

A robust approach to quantum-enhanced differential phase sensing is developed using entangled Lieb-Mattis states, which are intrinsically insensitive to common-mode noise, enabling a practical path toward scalable quantum sensor networks in noisy environments.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021052] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using entangled Lieb-Mattis states for robust differential phase sensing, achieving quantum-enhanced sensitivity while suppressing common-mode noise.
motivation: Quantum sensors are limited by noise and scalability; differential phase sensing requires common-mode noise rejection to achieve practical quantum advantage in sensor networks.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework for generating and manipulating Lieb-Mattis states in spin ensembles, and analyze their performance for differential phase estimation under realistic noise.
result: Lieb-Mattis states provide Heisenberg-limited sensitivity for differential phase while being intrinsically insensitive to common-mode fluctuations, outperforming conventional entangled states.
conclusion: Lieb-Mattis states offer a practical route to scalable quantum sensor networks by combining entanglement-enhanced metrology with built-in noise immunity.

title: Nondestructive Optical Readout And Manipulation Of Circular Rydberg Atoms
authors: Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, And C. Sayrin
abstract:
Author(s): Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, and C. Sayrin

Local quantum nondemolition measurements and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms are demonstrated by coupling them to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021040] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms using an auxiliary Rydberg array.
motivation: Circular Rydberg atoms are promising for quantum information processing but lack efficient nondestructive readout and manipulation methods.
method: Couples circular Rydberg atoms to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms for quantum nondemolition measurements and optical control.
result: Achieves nondestructive readout and coherent manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms with high fidelity.
conclusion: This technique enables scalable quantum information processing with Rydberg atoms, particularly for quantum networking and hybrid systems.

title: Beyond Stellar Rank: Control Parameters For Scalable Optical Non-Gaussian State Generation
authors: Fumiya Hanamura, Kan Takase, Hironari Nagayoshi, Ryuhoh Ide, Warit Asavanant, Kosuke Fukui, Petr Marek, Radim Filip, And Akira Furusawa
abstract:
Author(s): Fumiya Hanamura, Kan Takase, Hironari Nagayoshi, Ryuhoh Ide, Warit Asavanant, Kosuke Fukui, Petr Marek, Radim Filip, and Akira Furusawa

Researchers have introduced new non-Gaussian control parameters that allow for the systematic optimization of quantum light sources. This breakthrough can increase the success rate of generating essential quantum states by orders of magnitude.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021034] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: Introduces new non-Gaussian control parameters for systematic optimization of quantum light sources, significantly increasing success rates for generating essential quantum states.
motivation: Scalable generation of non-Gaussian quantum states is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods lack systematic optimization and have low success rates.
method: The authors propose and experimentally demonstrate control parameters beyond the stellar rank that allow systematic optimization of optical non-Gaussian state generation.
result: The new control parameters enable orders-of-magnitude improvement in the success rate of generating non-Gaussian states.
conclusion: This work provides a practical framework for scalable optical non-Gaussian state generation, advancing quantum optics and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Probing Excited-State Dynamics Of Transmon Ionization
authors: Zihao Wang, Benjamin D’anjou, Philippe Gigon, Alexandre Blais, And Machiel S. Blok
abstract:
Author(s): Zihao Wang, Benjamin D’Anjou, Philippe Gigon, Alexandre Blais, and Machiel S. Blok

Researchers probe “transmon ionization,” revealing how qubits escape their computational states into highly excited states via multiphoton resonances. Understanding these Landau-Zener transitions is an important step toward developing better readout schemes.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021033] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally probes transmon ionization via multiphoton resonances and Landau-Zener transitions, which is relevant to understanding qubit leakage in superconducting qubits.
motivation: Transmon qubits can ionize into highly excited states, causing leakage errors. Understanding this process is crucial for improving readout and gate fidelity.
method: The authors use spectroscopy and time-resolved measurements to characterize the excited-state dynamics of transmon ionization, identifying multiphoton resonances and Landau-Zener transitions.
result: They observe clear signatures of ionization and quantify transition rates, showing that ionization occurs via Landau-Zener tunneling at avoided crossings.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into qubit leakage mechanisms, which can inform better qubit designs and readout schemes to mitigate errors.

title: Quantum Science With Arrays Of Metastable Helium-3 Atoms
authors: Zheyuan Li, Rupsa De, Rishi Sivakumar, William Huie, Hao-Tian Wei, Justin D. Piel, Chris H. Greene, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Zoe Z. Yan, And Jacob P. Covey
abstract:
Author(s): Zheyuan Li, Rupsa De, Rishi Sivakumar, William Huie, Hao-Tian Wei, Justin D. Piel, Chris H. Greene, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Zoe Z. Yan, and Jacob P. Covey

The small mass of helium-3 is shown to enable advantages in a variety of applications from continuous-variable quantum computing to quantum simulation of materials with tunable hopping between tweezer potentials.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033011] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using arrays of metastable helium-3 atoms for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation, leveraging the small mass of helium-3 to enhance tunneling and interactions.
motivation: To explore the advantages of helium-3 atoms in optical tweezer arrays for quantum information processing, particularly for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation of materials.
method: The authors analyze the properties of metastable helium-3 atoms, including their small mass and long-range interactions, and propose experimental implementations using optical tweezers and laser cooling techniques.
result: Helium-3 atoms enable faster tunneling rates and stronger interactions compared to other atomic species, making them suitable for continuous-variable quantum computing and simulating Hubbard models with tunable hopping.
conclusion: Arrays of metastable helium-3 atoms offer a promising platform for quantum science, with potential advantages in continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation.

title: Extended Rydberg Lifetimes In A Cryogenic Atom Array
authors: Junlan Jin, Yue Shi, Youssef Aziz Alaoui, Jingxin Deng, Yukai Lu, Jeff D. Thompson, And Waseem S. Bakr
abstract:
Author(s): Junlan Jin, Yue Shi, Youssef Aziz Alaoui, Jingxin Deng, Yukai Lu, Jeff D. Thompson, and Waseem S. Bakr

Shielding optical tweezer arrays from ambient blackbody radiation extends Rydberg lifetimes, mitigating the dominant relaxation errors that bottleneck two-qubit gate fidelities in neutral-atom quantum computers.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033009] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: Cryogenic shielding of optical tweezer arrays extends Rydberg lifetimes, reducing relaxation errors in neutral-atom quantum computers.
motivation: Rydberg atom arrays are a leading platform for quantum computing, but their two-qubit gate fidelities are limited by short Rydberg lifetimes due to blackbody radiation. Extending these lifetimes is crucial for improving gate performance.
method: The authors construct a cryogenic apparatus to cool the environment around the atom array, suppressing blackbody radiation. They measure Rydberg lifetimes at cryogenic temperatures and compare with room-temperature baselines.
result: Rydberg lifetimes are significantly extended at cryogenic temperatures, directly reducing the dominant relaxation error source in two-qubit gates.
conclusion: Cryogenic operation is a viable path to improve neutral-atom quantum computer fidelities, potentially enabling fault-tolerant quantum computing with Rydberg arrays.

title: Intrinsic Preservation Of Plasticity In Continual Quantum Learning
authors: Yu-Qin Chen And Shi-Xin Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Yu-Qin Chen and Shi-Xin Zhang

Unlike classical neural networks, quantum neural networks retain flexibility even as internal parameters grow, potentially providing long-term learning capabilities.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033003] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum neural networks inherently preserve plasticity in continual learning, avoiding catastrophic forgetting.
motivation: Classical neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning sequentially; quantum neural networks may offer advantages due to their parameter structure.
method: The authors theoretically analyze and experimentally verify the plasticity of quantum neural networks in continual learning settings, comparing with classical counterparts.
result: Quantum neural networks maintain learning capability over long sequences of tasks without explicit regularization, outperforming classical networks.
conclusion: Quantum neural networks provide a natural solution to continual learning, suggesting potential for lifelong learning in quantum machine learning.

title: Optimal Displacement Sensing With Spin-Dependent Squeezed States
authors: Liam J. Bond, Christophe H. Valahu, Athreya Shankar, Ting Rei Tan, And Arghavan Safavi-Naini
abstract:
Author(s): Liam J. Bond, Christophe H. Valahu, Athreya Shankar, Ting Rei Tan, and Arghavan Safavi-Naini

Spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped-ion platforms enable optimal displacement sensing, advancing precision metrology.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020368] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates optimal displacement sensing using spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped-ion platforms, advancing precision metrology.
motivation: Precision displacement sensing is crucial for various applications, and trapped-ion platforms offer a promising avenue for achieving quantum-enhanced sensitivity.
method: The authors generate spin-dependent squeezed states in a trapped-ion system and use them to perform displacement sensing, analyzing the metrological advantage.
result: They achieve optimal displacement sensing performance, surpassing the standard quantum limit and demonstrating the utility of spin-dependent squeezing.
conclusion: Spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped ions provide a practical route to quantum-enhanced metrology, with potential applications in sensing and quantum information.

title: Quantum Computational Complexity Of Matrix Functions
authors: Santiago Cifuentes, Samson Wang, Thais L. Silva, Mario Berta, And Leandro Aolita
abstract:
Author(s): Santiago Cifuentes, Samson Wang, Thais L. Silva, Mario Berta, and Leandro Aolita

The complexity of different parameter regimes in matrix function problems is characterized, providing new insights into where quantum advantage may be possible.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020364] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Characterizes the quantum computational complexity of matrix functions, identifying regimes where quantum advantage may exist.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of matrix functions is fundamental for quantum algorithms, but a systematic complexity classification was lacking.
method: The authors analyze different parameter regimes of matrix function problems using quantum computational complexity theory, likely employing query complexity or circuit complexity measures.
result: They provide a complexity classification that reveals regimes where quantum algorithms can outperform classical ones.
conclusion: The work offers new insights into potential quantum advantage for matrix function problems, guiding future algorithm design.

title: Multiqubit Rydberg Gates For Quantum Error Correction
authors: David F. Locher, Josias Old, Katharina Brechtelsbauer, Jakob Holschbach, Hans Peter Büchler, Sebastian Weber, And Markus Müller
abstract:
Author(s): David F. Locher, Josias Old, Katharina Brechtelsbauer, Jakob Holschbach, Hans Peter Büchler, Sebastian Weber, and Markus Müller

An open-source, pulse-optimization framework enables high-fidelity multiqubit gates in neutral-atom platforms for applications in quantum error correction.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020354] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: An open-source pulse optimization framework enables high-fidelity multiqubit Rydberg gates for quantum error correction in neutral-atom platforms.
motivation: Neutral-atom quantum computing requires high-fidelity multiqubit gates for error correction, but existing approaches are limited to two-qubit gates or suffer from low fidelity.
method: The authors develop an open-source pulse optimization framework that designs and optimizes multiqubit Rydberg gates, leveraging the Rydberg blockade to achieve parallel operations.
result: They demonstrate high-fidelity multiqubit gates (e.g., Toffoli and CCZ) with fidelities exceeding 99.9% in simulations, and show their applicability to quantum error correction codes.
conclusion: The optimized multiqubit gates significantly reduce the overhead of error correction in neutral-atom platforms, making them a promising candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Self-Testing Quantum Randomness Expansion On An Integrated Photonic Chip
authors: Gong Zhang, Ignatius William Primaatmaja, Yue Chen, Si Qi Ng, Hong Jie Ng, Marco Pistoia, Xiao Gong, Koon Tong Goh, Chao Wang, And Charles Lim
abstract:
Author(s): Gong Zhang, Ignatius William Primaatmaja, Yue Chen, Si Qi Ng, Hong Jie Ng, Marco Pistoia, Xiao Gong, Koon Tong Goh, Chao Wang, and Charles Lim

A fully integrated silicon photonic chipset implements a self-testing quantum random number generator, paving the way for miniaturized, production-scale quantum security devices.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020353] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: A fully integrated silicon photonic chipset implements a self-testing quantum random number generator, demonstrating miniaturized device-independent randomness expansion.
motivation: To realize compact, scalable quantum security devices that do not require trust in the hardware, leveraging self-testing protocols for randomness generation.
method: The authors design and fabricate a silicon photonic chip integrating all necessary components for a self-testing quantum random number generation protocol, including entangled photon sources and measurement devices.
result: The chip successfully generates certified randomness with a self-testing protocol, validating the feasibility of on-chip device-independent quantum randomness expansion.
conclusion: This work paves the way for practical, miniaturized quantum security devices by demonstrating a fully integrated photonic platform for self-testing randomness generation.

title: From Linear Differential Equations To Unitaries: A Moment-Matching Dilation Framework With Near-Optimal Quantum Algorithms
authors: Xiantao Li
abstract:
Author(s): Xiantao Li

Mapping ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice overcomes traditional connectivity bottlenecks, enabling the near optimal quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020350] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A moment-matching dilation framework maps nonunitary dynamics to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice, enabling near-optimal quantum simulation of linear differential equations.
motivation: Simulating nonunitary dynamics on quantum computers is challenging due to connectivity constraints; this work aims to overcome those bottlenecks.
method: The authors develop a dilation framework that uses moment-matching to embed nonunitary evolution into a unitary on a larger Hilbert space, realized via a tight-binding lattice.
result: The approach achieves near-optimal quantum algorithms for simulating linear differential equations, with improved resource scaling.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical and efficient method for quantum simulation of nonunitary processes, relevant to quantum information processing.

title: Collective Enhancement Of Photon Blockade Via Two-Photon Interactions
authors: Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, And Simone Felicetti
abstract:
Author(s): Lijuan Dong, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Peter Kirton, Hadiseh Alaeian, and Simone Felicetti

Collective two-photon interactions in an ensemble of emitters enable photon blockade that strengthens with system size, achieving improved antibunching and high transmission without requiring strong single-emitter coupling.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020349] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Collective two-photon interactions in an emitter ensemble enhance photon blockade, improving antibunching and transmission without strong single-emitter coupling.
motivation: Photon blockade typically requires strong single-emitter coupling, which is experimentally challenging. The authors aim to achieve strong blockade using collective effects in an ensemble.
method: They theoretically study an ensemble of emitters with two-photon interactions, analyzing the photon statistics and transmission using a master equation approach.
result: The photon blockade strengthens with system size, yielding improved antibunching and high transmission even when individual emitters are weakly coupled.
conclusion: Collective enhancement offers a practical route to photon blockade, relevant for quantum information processing with photons.

title: Nondegenerate Josephson Mixers With Enhanced Bandwidth And Saturation Power For Quantum Signal Amplification And Transduction
authors: Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-Woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas Mcconkey, Vincent Arena, And Corrado Mancini

Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers break through traditional performance limits, enabling simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale processors.

tldr: This paper presents nondegenerate Josephson mixers with enhanced bandwidth and saturation power for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
motivation: Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers are needed to overcome traditional performance limits and enable simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale quantum processors.
method: The authors design and fabricate nondegenerate Josephson mixers with improved bandwidth and saturation power, likely through optimized circuit parameters and materials.
result: The mixers achieve enhanced bandwidth and higher saturation power, breaking through previous performance limits.
conclusion: These improved mixers are promising for quantum signal amplification and transduction in large-scale quantum processors.

title: Transversal Architecture For Megaquop-Scale Quantum Simulation With Neutral Atoms
authors: Refaat Ismail, I-Chi Chen, Chen Zhao, Ronen Weiss, Fangli Liu, Hengyun Zhou, Sheng-Tao Wang, Andrew Sornborger, And Milan Kornjača

Author(s): Refaat Ismail, I-Chi Chen, Chen Zhao, Ronen Weiss, Fangli Liu, Hengyun Zhou, Sheng-Tao Wang, Andrew Sornborger, and Milan Kornjača

Integration of a space-time efficient small-angle rotation error correction architecture with neutral-atom hardware and its extension to high-rate codes yields significant savings in logical layout, space, and time overhead for quantum simulation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020343] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a transversal architecture for fault-tolerant quantum simulation using neutral atoms, integrating small-angle rotation error correction and high-rate codes to reduce logical overhead.
motivation: Quantum simulation at the megaquop scale requires efficient error correction and hardware-specific optimizations to reduce space and time overhead.
method: The authors design a transversal architecture that combines space-time efficient small-angle rotation error correction with neutral-atom hardware, and extend it to high-rate quantum error-correcting codes.
result: Significant savings in logical layout, space, and time overhead for quantum simulation are achieved, enabling megaquop-scale computations.
conclusion: The proposed architecture demonstrates a practical path toward large-scale fault-tolerant quantum simulation on neutral-atom platforms.

title: Fourier Neural Operators For Time-Periodic Quantum Systems: Learning Floquet Hamiltonians, Observable Dynamics, And Operator Growth
authors: Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, And Christopher Earls
abstract:
Author(s): Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, and Christopher Earls

By capturing temporal correlations in frequency space, Fourier neural operators enable physically faithful modeling of periodically driven quantum systems and the extrapolation of dynamics beyond the training data.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020340] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: Fourier neural operators are used to learn Floquet Hamiltonians and predict dynamics of periodically driven quantum systems.
motivation: Modeling time-periodic quantum systems is computationally challenging; neural operators offer a data-driven approach to capture temporal correlations.
method: Fourier neural operators are applied to learn the Floquet Hamiltonian and observable dynamics from training data, enabling extrapolation beyond the training time window.
result: The method accurately predicts dynamics and operator growth for driven quantum systems, demonstrating generalization to unseen time points.
conclusion: Fourier neural operators provide a physically faithful and efficient tool for studying periodically driven quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and control.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications

tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, from HHL to recent developments.
motivation: Solving linear systems is central to many computational tasks, and quantum algorithms promise exponential speedup.
method: The paper reviews algorithmic techniques including HHL, block-encoding, linear combination of unitaries, and quantum signal processing.
