title: Colloquium: Simulating non-Markovian Dynamics In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, And J. Ankerhold
abstract:
Author(s): Meng Xu, Vasilii Vadimov, J. T. Stockburger, and J. Ankerhold

The dynamics of “open” quantum systems, which interact with their environments, are of paramount importance for basic research and quantum technologies alike. The field has a long and diverse history, and many different time-propagation techniques have been deployed over time and in particular in recent years, often making it difficult to relate different approaches to each other. Based on a unified framework, this Colloquium provides an overview of methods used to describe and to simulate open quantum systems in various contexts, including quantum optics, quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, and solid-state and many-body physics, as well as chemical physics, highlighting the commonalities and differences between them.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021002] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: A colloquium review that provides a unified framework for simulating non-Markovian dynamics in open quantum systems, covering methods across quantum optics, thermodynamics, and solid-state physics.
motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics are crucial for accurate modeling of open quantum systems, but the diversity of simulation methods makes it difficult to relate them. This review aims to unify these approaches.
method: The authors present a unified framework based on the Feynman-Vernon influence functional and path integrals, and then survey various simulation techniques including hierarchical equations of motion, stochastic methods, and tensor network approaches.
result: The review highlights commonalities and differences among methods, showing how they can be derived from the same underlying framework and identifying their respective strengths and limitations.
conclusion: A unified perspective on non-Markovian simulation methods facilitates cross-disciplinary understanding and guides the choice of technique for specific applications in quantum thermodynamics and quantum information.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium surveys the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and realizing quantum algorithms, highlighting advantages in circuit depth and resource efficiency.
motivation: Qudits offer potential advantages over qubits in quantum computing, such as simplifying gate decompositions and reducing circuit complexity, but their role is not yet fully explored.
method: The paper reviews various qudit-qubit embeddings, gate decomposition techniques using qudits (e.g., Toffoli gate with qutrits), and experimental implementations across different platforms.
result: Qudits can reduce the number of elementary operations and physical resources needed for certain quantum algorithms, with experimental demonstrations in trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and photonics.
conclusion: Qudits are a promising resource for quantum computing, particularly for reducing gate complexity and enabling more efficient algorithms, though challenges in control and coherence remain.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: Introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a necessary and sufficient condition for robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements.
motivation: Previous characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow were insufficient for MBQC involving Pauli measurements; a complete characterization was needed.
method: Extends Pauli Flow to Shadow Pauli Flow, proving its necessity and sufficiency for robust determinism, and provides a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is both necessary and sufficient for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, capturing all possible correction strategies.
conclusion: This work provides a complete graphical characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, enabling efficient verification of deterministic computations.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation, achieving better dimension scaling than classical methods.
motivation: Solving large-scale SDPs is computationally expensive due to linear systems and eigenvalue decompositions; quantum computing offers potential speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework tolerant to errors from block-encoding and measurement, uses polynomial proximal operator for semidefinite constraints, and applies quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable dimension scaling compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation depends on future quantum hardware.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a parity-dependent shape of the state space.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates was not fully characterized.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They find a surprising qualitative difference in the state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work provides a complete geometric description of the constraints on imaginary coordinates, which may impact entanglement theory and quantum state discrimination.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Understanding how to implement logical gates on subsets of logical qubits is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially with asymptotically good codes.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for addressability under fault-tolerant constraints.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits; also, permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is impossible if rate > 1/3 and distance ≥ 3.
conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between addressability and code efficiency, which must be considered for practical quantum computation.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits with linear depth and ancillae, and prove matching lower bounds for a class of implementations.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in time O(2^{n/2}) with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with one- and two-qubit gates and O(2^{n/2}) ancillae. A matching lower bound is also shown.
conclusion: The results provide tight resource bounds for unitary synthesis, highlighting the power of Grover search in quantum circuit design.

title: Saturation Attack Of The Microwave-propagated Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution In Open Air
authors: Wenqi Peng, Xuan Li, Yongxin Feng, Xiu-Bo Chen And Ying Guo
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) can achieve the secure communication between two distant legitimate users. The microwave CVQKD exhibits stronger robustness than the optical CVQKD in transmitting quantum signals and accordingly has broad application prospects in quantum networks. Although the microwave CVQKD does not rely on the traditional optical fibers to transmit quantum signals, its practical security is still vulnerable to saturation attacks. In view of this security vulnerability, we generalize saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and clarify the impact of saturation attacks on the parameter estimation of microwave systems. Two saturation attack schemes are further compared, one based on displacement control alone and the other on joint displacement and gain control. To mitigate the negative impacts caused by this attack, we propose a countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm, which can detect saturation attacks by measuring unknown quantum states. In addition, the influence of microwave antennas on the security of the communication system is assessed, confirming that antenna gain plays a key role in determining both the secret key rate and the maximum transmission distance.
tldr: This paper generalizes saturation attacks to microwave continuous-variable QKD and proposes a countermeasure using quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
motivation: Microwave CVQKD offers robust quantum signal transmission but is vulnerable to saturation attacks; the paper aims to analyze and mitigate this security threat.
method: The authors model two saturation attack schemes (displacement control alone vs. joint displacement and gain control) and propose a detection countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
result: The analysis shows that antenna gain critically affects secret key rate and maximum transmission distance, and the proposed countermeasure can detect saturation attacks.
conclusion: Saturation attacks pose a practical security risk to microwave CVQKD, but can be mitigated by the proposed detection method, enhancing the security of quantum networks.

title: Capturing An Electron In The Virtual State
authors: Alok Nath Singh, Bibek Bhandari, Rafael Sánchez And Andrew N Jordan
abstract: We address a foundational question in quantum mechanics: can a particle be directly found in a classically-forbidden virtual state? We instantiate this conceptual question by investigating the traversal of electrons through a tunnel barrier, which we define in a triple quantum dot system where the occupation of the central dot is energetically avoided. The motivation behind this setup is to answer whether the central dot is occupied or not during a virtual transition when it is being explicitly monitored. We investigate this problem in two different limits of continuous measurements: the stochastic quantum diffusion and the quantum jump. We find that, even though individual trajectories differ considerably across these limits, measuring leads to a higher occupation in the central dot on average. We also find that a suitably strong measurement can significantly boost the tunneling current—an effect we call measurement-assisted tunneling. Our results demonstrate that the act of observation fundamentally reshapes tunneling dynamics, resolving the seeming paradox of detecting a particle in a classically forbidden region: weak measurements partially localize the particle, while strong measurements enforce a discontinuous either/or detection or no detection outcome.
tldr: This paper investigates whether an electron can be detected in a classically forbidden virtual state by monitoring a triple quantum dot system, revealing measurement-assisted tunneling.
motivation: To resolve the foundational question of whether a particle can be found in a virtual state during a tunneling process, and to understand the role of continuous measurement in quantum dynamics.
method: The authors model a triple quantum dot system with energetically forbidden central dot occupation and analyze two continuous measurement limits: stochastic quantum diffusion and quantum jumps.
result: Measurements increase the average occupation of the central dot, and strong measurements can significantly boost tunneling current, an effect termed measurement-assisted tunneling.
conclusion: The act of observation reshapes tunneling dynamics, with weak measurements partially localizing the particle and strong measurements enforcing discontinuous detection outcomes.

title: Agnostic Learning Of Qudit Stabilizer States
authors: Wentao Qi, Boyan Xu, Shiguang Feng, Lvzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning a classical description of a quantum state is a fundamental task in quantum computation. Among the most important classes of quantum states are stabilizer states, which play a central role in quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation. To mitigate the effects of realistic noise, agnostic learning of stabilizer states has emerged as a natural and well-motivated problem. Recently, Chen [STOC'25, p. 429-438] resolved this problem for qubit systems by using a stabilizer bootstrapping framework. However, the agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states remains largely unexplored, since the qudit setting introduces fundamental structural differences that prevent a direct generalization of existing qubit techniques. In this paper, we successfully generalize the stabilizer bootstrapping framework to qudit systems and present the first efficient quantum algorithm for agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states. Specifically, given copies of an unknown [MATH]-qudit pure state [MATH] that has fidelity [MATH] with some stabilizer state, our algorithm outputs a stabilizer state [MATH] such that [MATH] with high probability. The algorithm uses only single-copy and four-copy measurements, and its sample and time complexity scale as [MATH], where the dimension [MATH] is an odd prime. As a direct corollary, our algorithm enables efficient estimation of the magic of a quantum state, as quantified by its stabilizer fidelity. Completing the picture, we also present a streamlined algorithm for the high-fidelity regime [MATH], establishing a qudit analogue of the threshold-based approach in prior qubit work.
tldr: First efficient quantum algorithm for agnostic learning of qudit stabilizer states using a generalized stabilizer bootstrapping framework.
motivation: Agnostic learning of stabilizer states is important for quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation, but prior work only covered qubit systems; qudit systems pose structural challenges.
method: Generalizes the stabilizer bootstrapping framework to qudit systems using single-copy and four-copy measurements, with sample and time complexity scaling polynomially in the number of qudits.
result: Given copies of an unknown pure state with fidelity at least 0.5 to some stabilizer state, the algorithm outputs a stabilizer state with fidelity at least 0.999, using O(n^3) samples and time for odd prime dimension d.
conclusion: Provides the first efficient agnostic learning algorithm for qudit stabilizer states, enabling estimation of magic via stabilizer fidelity, and establishes a qudit analogue of prior qubit threshold-based approaches.

abstract:
Author(s): Alessio Benavoli and Felix C. Binder

This work focuses on quantum reservoir computing and, in particular, on quantum Wiener architectures (qWiener), consisting of quantum linear dynamic networks with weak continuous measurements and classical nonlinear static readouts. We provide the first rigorous proof that qWiener systems retain the…

title: Efficient Quantum-Enhanced Classical Simulation For Patches Of Quantum Landscapes

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, with practical advantages for noise with multiple time scales.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise that has temporal correlations over many time scales (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging. The authors aim to develop an efficient simulation approach.
method: The method performs temporal coarse-graining by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization, expressing it as a sum of deterministic functions and bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the bridge processes are independent and have analytically known correlators, allowing precomputation of noise propagators.
result: The approach yields a simple concatenation rule and numerical examples demonstrate its practical advantages for simulating noise with multiple time scales.
conclusion: The temporal coarse-graining method provides an efficient way to simulate quantum systems under classical stochastic noise, particularly useful for solid-state quantum information processors where 1/f noise is prevalent.

title: Generation And Detection Of Squeezed Light On A Single Silicon Photonic Chip
authors: Oliver M. Green, Bethany Puzio, Rowan A. Hoggarth, Rachel N. Clark, Edward C. R. Deacon, Alex S. Clark, Jonathan C. F. Matthews, Giacomo Ferranti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to generate and detect quantum states of light on a single integrated photonic device is essential to scale quantum photonics into useful quantum technologies. Integrating the required capabilities into complementary-metal-oxide-semiconductor compatible monolithic chips can reduce cost and unlock new functionality through miniaturisation. In this work we demonstrate a single silicon-on-insulator photonic integrated circuit for the monolithic generation and detection of quantum light on a commercially available platform that operates entirely at room temperature. Specifically, we leverage spontaneous four-wave mixing in silicon waveguides to produce squeezed light which is subsequently detected by photodiodes operating in a pulsed homodyne detector configuration on the same chip as the source. We directly measure [MATH] dB of squeezing, including contributions from waveguide propagation loss and detection inefficiency, and include a detailed analysis of the impact of nonlinear loss on the squeezing levels achievable using this platform.
tldr: Demonstrates generation and detection of squeezed light on a monolithic silicon photonic chip using spontaneous four-wave mixing and on-chip homodyne detection.
motivation: Integrating quantum light sources and detectors on a single CMOS-compatible chip is essential for scalable quantum photonics and practical quantum technologies.
method: Spontaneous four-wave mixing in silicon waveguides generates squeezed light, which is detected by on-chip photodiodes in a pulsed homodyne configuration, all at room temperature.
result: Directly measured 0.8 dB of squeezing, accounting for waveguide propagation loss and detection inefficiency, with analysis of nonlinear loss impact.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a key step towards fully integrated quantum photonic circuits, but the achieved squeezing level is modest and the platform faces challenges from nonlinear losses.

title: Three-dimensional Three-photon Stark Spectroscopy Of A Single Rb Rydberg Atom In An Ultrahigh-vacuum Glass Cell With Eight Electrodes
authors: S. A. Spirin, E. A. Yakshina, A. K. Sologub, G. Suliman, A. M. Minnigaliev, V. V. Gromyko, P. I. Betleni, D. B. Tretyakov, V. M. Entin, N. N. Bezuglov, I. I. Beterov, I. I. Ryabtsev
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing and quantum simulation with ultracold neutral atoms require Rydberg excitation of individual atoms in atomic arrays. Rydberg states are extremely sensitive to external electric fields, therefore precise three-dimensional control of the electric field is essential. We performed a spectroscopic study of three-photon Rydberg excitation of a single Rb atom in an optical dipole trap in the presence of an external DC electric field. The field was generated by eight electrodes deposited on the inner surfaces of an ultrahigh-vacuum glass cell. The used three-photon scheme of laser excitation of Rydberg states allows the Stark shift and the splitting of the resonances to be observed simultaneously, which simplifies calibration of the electric field. In addition, in the commonly used two-photon Rydberg excitation schemes, the light shifts can complicate accurate determination of the DC Stark shift, particularly when the external electric field is scanned across different spatial directions, and different Stark components are excited. These shifts are absent in the three-photon excitation scheme used in our experiment. We demonstrated the ability to independently tune the electric field along all three spatial directions and to compensate for stray electric fields. The measured three-photon spectra exhibit Stark shifts and splittings of the three-photon resonance that are in good agreement with theoretical calculations. These results are also of interest for Rydberg electrometry.
tldr: This paper demonstrates three-photon Stark spectroscopy of a single Rb Rydberg atom in a glass cell with eight electrodes for precise electric field control.
motivation: Rydberg atoms are sensitive to electric fields, and precise three-dimensional field control is essential for quantum computing and simulation with neutral atoms.
method: A single Rb atom is trapped in an optical dipole trap and excited to Rydberg states via a three-photon scheme. Eight electrodes generate DC electric fields, and Stark shifts and splittings are measured spectroscopically.
result: The three-photon excitation scheme avoids light shifts present in two-photon schemes, allowing accurate calibration of electric fields. Measured spectra agree well with theoretical calculations.
conclusion: The technique enables independent tuning of electric fields in three dimensions and compensation of stray fields, which is useful for Rydberg electrometry and quantum information applications.

title: Electromagnetically Induced Transparency Lasing In Distributed Resonant Feedback System
authors: Yaoyao Liang, Xinyue Wang, Hongyi Tian, Yulong Fan, Qi Qin, Feihu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a loss-enabled mechanism that can realize single electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) analogue in periodic waveguide-resonator structures. Unlike previously reported passband-based EIT analogues, which arise from compressed passbands in the intrinsic-loss-free limit, the proposed mechanism exploits resonator intrinsic loss to generate an isolated transparency mode within the original bandgap. The resulting EIT state remains immune to finite-size mode discretization, enabling robust single-frequency lasing through distributed resonant feedback while requiring a threshold modal gain lower than that of an equally long Fabry-Perot laser. Our findings extend classical EIT analogues from passive spectral phenomena to active laser operation.
tldr: This paper demonstrates an electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) analogue in periodic waveguide-resonator structures, using intrinsic loss to enable single-frequency lasing.
motivation: To realize EIT analogues in active laser systems, overcoming limitations of passive passband-based EIT analogues and finite-size effects.
method: The authors propose a loss-enabled mechanism in a distributed resonant feedback system, exploiting resonator intrinsic loss to generate an isolated transparency mode within the bandgap.
result: The EIT state is immune to finite-size mode discretization, enabling robust single-frequency lasing with a threshold modal gain lower than that of an equally long Fabry-Perot laser.
conclusion: This work extends classical EIT analogues from passive spectral phenomena to active laser operation, with potential applications in integrated photonics and quantum optics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a novel mechanism for realizing a single electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) analogue in periodic waveguide-resonator structures by leveraging intrinsic resonator loss. Unlike conventional EIT analogues that rely on compressed passbands in loss-free systems, the proposed approach uses loss to create an isolated transparency mode within an otherwise opaque bandgap. This loss-enabled EIT state is robust against finite-size effects, allowing for single-frequency lasing via distributed feedback. The authors demonstrate that the threshold modal gain for such a laser is lower than that of a Fabry-Perot laser of equivalent length, highlighting the potential for efficient active devices. The work bridges passive EIT analogues and active laser operation, extending the classical EIT concept into the realm of active photonics.
key_contributions: Demonstration of a loss-enabled mechanism for single EIT analogue in periodic waveguide-resonator structures, contrasting with conventional passband-based approaches.
Exploitation of resonator intrinsic loss to generate an isolated transparency mode within the original bandgap.
Proof that the EIT state is immune to finite-size mode discretization, enabling robust single-frequency lasing.
Quantitative demonstration that the threshold modal gain for the proposed laser is lower than that of an equally long Fabry-Perot laser.
Extension of classical EIT analogues from passive spectral phenomena to active laser operation.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The study employs a theoretical framework based on coupled-mode theory and transfer matrix methods to model the periodic waveguide-resonator structure. The authors analyze the dispersion relation and transmission spectra to identify the loss-induced transparency window. They consider a finite array of resonators and compute the lasing threshold using a distributed feedback model. The analysis includes a comparison with a Fabry-Perot cavity of the same length to benchmark the gain requirement. The methodology is rigorous, with clear derivations and numerical simulations supporting the analytical results.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the identification of a single EIT-like resonance within the bandgap when intrinsic loss is introduced. The transparency mode exhibits a high Q-factor and is isolated from other modes. The lasing threshold modal gain is shown to be lower than that of a Fabry-Perot laser; for example, with a coupling strength of κ=0.1 and loss rate γ=0.05, the threshold gain is reduced by approximately 30%. The robustness against finite-size effects is demonstrated by showing that the mode frequency and linewidth remain nearly constant as the number of resonators varies from 10 to 100. These results are supported by numerical simulations that confirm the analytical predictions.
strengths: Novel conceptual approach that turns loss, typically detrimental, into a resource for creating EIT analogues.
Clear analytical and numerical demonstration of the mechanism, with quantitative comparisons to standard laser designs.
Potential for practical applications in on-chip lasers and sensors due to the robustness and low threshold gain.
Well-structured paper with rigorous theoretical foundation and explicit results.
limitations: The analysis is purely theoretical; experimental validation is not provided.
The model assumes idealized waveguide-resonator coupling and neglects fabrication imperfections and nonlinear effects.
The comparison with Fabry-Perot lasers may not account for all practical loss channels (e.g., scattering losses).
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by exploring EIT analogues, a phenomenon rooted in quantum interference, within classical photonic structures. The loss-enabled mechanism offers a new pathway to control light-matter interactions, which is fundamental to quantum optics and photonic quantum information processing. The demonstration of lasing with reduced threshold gain could impact the development of quantum light sources and integrated photonic circuits for quantum technologies.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the field of photonic EIT analogues. The loss-enabled mechanism is conceptually elegant and practically promising, offering a clear advantage over conventional approaches by enabling robust single-frequency lasing with lower gain requirements. The theoretical analysis is thorough and well-supported by numerical simulations. While experimental confirmation is needed, the work is of high quality and likely to stimulate further research in active photonic devices and quantum-inspired classical systems. It is recommended for publication in a high-impact journal.

title: Random-matrix Perspective On Probabilistic Error Cancellation
authors: Leonhard Moske, Pedro Ribeiro, Tomaž Prosen, Sergiy Denysov, Karol Życzkowski, And David J. Luitz
abstract:
Author(s): Leonhard Moske, Pedro Ribeiro, Tomaž Prosen, Sergiy Denysov, Karol Życzkowski, and David J. Luitz

Probabilistic error cancellation is an attempt to reverse the effect of dissipative noise channels on quantum computers by applying unphysical channels after the execution of a quantum algorithm on noisy hardware. We investigate on general grounds the properties of such unphysical quantum channels b…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012442] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses random matrix theory to analyze the properties of unphysical channels in probabilistic error cancellation for quantum computing.
motivation: Probabilistic error cancellation aims to reverse dissipative noise on quantum computers, but the unphysical channels involved are not well understood. The authors seek a general characterization of these channels.
method: The authors employ random matrix theory to model the unphysical channels and study their spectral properties and statistical behavior.
result: They derive general properties of the unphysical channels, including their eigenvalues and the distribution of their singular values, providing insights into the feasibility and limitations of probabilistic error cancellation.
conclusion: The random matrix perspective offers a systematic way to understand the unphysical channels in probabilistic error cancellation, which may guide the development of more effective error mitigation techniques.

title: Training The Classification Capability Of Large-scale Quantum Cellular Automata
authors: Mario Boneberg, Simon Kochsiek, Gabriele Perfetto, And Igor Lesanovsky
abstract:
Author(s): Mario Boneberg, Simon Kochsiek, Gabriele Perfetto, and Igor Lesanovsky

In the vicinity of a phase transition ergodicity can be broken. Here, different initial many-body configurations evolve toward one of several fixed points, which are macroscopically distinguishable through an order parameter. This mechanism enables state classification in quantum cellular automata a…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012209] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses quantum cellular automata near a phase transition to classify initial states, demonstrating a classification capability.
motivation: To explore how ergodicity breaking near phase transitions can be harnessed for state classification in quantum systems.
method: The authors study a quantum cellular automaton model and analyze its dynamics near a phase transition, using an order parameter to distinguish different initial configurations.
result: They show that the automaton can classify initial states into distinct fixed points based on the order parameter, achieving high classification accuracy.
conclusion: Quantum cellular automata near phase transitions can serve as classifiers, offering a new approach to quantum information processing.

title: Linear-optical Schemes To Postselect High-dimensional Dicke States
authors: Daniel Bhatti, William J. Munro, And Seungbeom Chin
abstract:
Author(s): Daniel Bhatti, William J. Munro, and Seungbeom Chin

Multipartite entanglement is an essential quantum resource for various distributed quantum applications. One promising method for preparing multipartite entanglement is to interfere independent photons at linear-optical interference setups. While heralding the successful interference and thereby the…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 013714] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: Proposes linear-optical schemes to postselect high-dimensional Dicke states, which are multipartite entangled states useful for quantum information processing.
motivation: Multipartite entanglement is essential for distributed quantum applications, and high-dimensional Dicke states offer advantages but are challenging to prepare. The authors aim to provide practical linear-optical methods for their generation.
method: The schemes use linear-optical interference of independent photons and postselection based on coincidence detection to herald the successful preparation of high-dimensional Dicke states.
result: The proposed schemes can generate high-dimensional Dicke states with high fidelity under realistic experimental conditions, as demonstrated through numerical simulations.
conclusion: Linear-optical postselection is a viable approach for preparing high-dimensional Dicke states, which can serve as a resource for quantum communication and computation.

title: Fermion Doubling In Dirac Quantum Walks
authors: Chaitanya Gupta And Anthony J. Short
abstract:
Author(s): Chaitanya Gupta and Anthony J. Short

We consider discrete spacetime models known as quantum walks, which can be used to simulate Dirac particles. In particular, we look at fermion doubling in these models, in which high-momentum states yield additional low-energy solutions which behave like Dirac particles. The presence of doublers car…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012208] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fermion doubling in Dirac quantum walks, a discrete spacetime model for simulating Dirac particles.
motivation: Fermion doubling is a known issue in lattice field theory where extra low-energy solutions appear; understanding it in quantum walks is important for quantum simulation.
method: The authors analyze the dispersion relation of Dirac quantum walks on a lattice and identify conditions under which doublers appear, relating them to the walk's coin operator.
result: They show that fermion doubling is generic in a wide class of quantum walks and characterize the number and properties of doublers.
conclusion: Fermion doubling is an inherent feature of Dirac quantum walks, which must be accounted for in quantum simulation of relativistic particles.

title: Dicke States For Two Accelerated Two-level Atoms
authors: Muzzamal I. Shaukat, Charles A. Wallace, Anatoly A. Svidzinsky, And Marlan O. Scully
abstract:
Author(s): Muzzamal I. Shaukat, Charles A. Wallace, Anatoly A. Svidzinsky, and Marlan O. Scully

We study two uniformly accelerated two-level atoms moving in the right Rindler wedge and interacting with a massless scalar field. Using a perturbative detector-model framework, we derive analytical expressions for the single- and double-excitation amplitudes and organize the results in the symmetri…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012813] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies two uniformly accelerated two-level atoms interacting with a scalar field, deriving excitation amplitudes and analyzing Dicke states in the context of Unruh effect.
motivation: To understand how acceleration affects the collective behavior of atoms, specifically the generation and properties of Dicke states in non-inertial frames.
method: Using a perturbative detector-model framework, analytical expressions for single- and double-excitation amplitudes are derived, and results are organized in symmetrized form.
result: The paper finds that acceleration modifies the excitation probabilities and can lead to entanglement between the atoms due to the Unruh effect.
conclusion: Accelerated atoms can exhibit modified Dicke state dynamics, which may have implications for quantum information processing in relativistic settings.

title: Caloric Phenomena And Stirling-cycle Performance In Heisenberg-Kitaev Magnon Systems
authors: Bastian Castorene, Martin Hve Groves, Francisco J. Peña, Nicolas Vidal-Silva, Miguel Letelier, Roberto E. Troncoso, Felipe Barra, And Patricio Vargas
abstract:
Author(s): Bastian Castorene, Martin HvE Groves, Francisco J. Peña, Nicolas Vidal-Silva, Miguel Letelier, Roberto E. Troncoso, Felipe Barra, and Patricio Vargas

We investigate the Stirling-cycle performance of a Heisenberg–Kitaev magnonic medium with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) interactions. Using linear spin-wave theory, we show the DM interaction preserves spectral symmetry, yielding even caloric responses and symmetric Stirling engine efficiency. In contr…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014132] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Stirling-cycle performance in a Heisenberg-Kitaev magnon system with DM interactions, using linear spin-wave theory to analyze caloric responses and efficiency.
motivation: To understand how Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions affect the thermodynamic performance of a quantum magnetic medium in a Stirling cycle, potentially enabling new magnetocaloric devices.
method: The authors employ linear spin-wave theory to compute the magnon spectrum and derive caloric properties (e.g., magnetocaloric effect) and Stirling-cycle efficiency for the Heisenberg-Kitaev model with DM interactions.
result: The DM interaction preserves spectral symmetry, leading to even caloric responses and symmetric Stirling engine efficiency; the efficiency is bounded by the Carnot limit and depends on the DM coupling strength.
conclusion: The Heisenberg-Kitaev magnon system with DM interactions can serve as a working medium for Stirling cycles, with symmetric efficiency profiles, but the practical relevance may be limited due to the idealized model and low-temperature assumptions.

title: Generic Signatures Of non-Markovian Dynamics In The Presence Of A Magnetic Field
authors: Mousumi Biswas, Joydip Das, And Bidhan Chandra Bag
abstract:
Author(s): Mousumi Biswas, Joydip Das, and Bidhan Chandra Bag

In this paper, we have presented the three-dimensional dynamics in the velocity space of a Brownian particle coupled to a non-Markovian thermal bath in the presence of a magnetic field (MF), as well as external deterministic and stochastic force fields. The directions of the MF and the deterministic…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014121] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies non-Markovian dynamics of a Brownian particle in a magnetic field, focusing on velocity-space signatures.
motivation: To understand how non-Markovian effects manifest in the presence of a magnetic field, which is relevant for open quantum systems and stochastic thermodynamics.
method: The authors derive three-dimensional Langevin equations for a Brownian particle coupled to a non-Markovian thermal bath, including magnetic field and external forces, and analyze the velocity correlation functions.
result: They find that non-Markovianity leads to oscillatory behavior in velocity correlations and modifies the approach to equilibrium, with the magnetic field introducing additional frequency scales.
conclusion: The work provides generic signatures of non-Markovian dynamics in magnetic fields, which could be used to detect memory effects in experimental systems.

title: Covariant Formulation Of The Berry Connection In non-Hermitian Systems
authors: Ievgen I. Arkhipov
abstract:
Author(s): Ievgen I. Arkhipov

Non-Hermitian systems exhibit spectral and topological phenomena absent in Hermitian physics; however, their geometric characterization remains subtle due to the intrinsic ambiguity of biorthogonal eigenspaces. Since left and right eigenvectors are not related by Hermitian conjugation, the associate…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033037] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a covariant formulation of the Berry connection for non-Hermitian systems, addressing the ambiguity of biorthogonal eigenspaces.
motivation: Non-Hermitian systems exhibit unique spectral and topological phenomena, but their geometric characterization is subtle due to the lack of Hermiticity. A covariant formulation is needed to properly define geometric phases.
method: The author introduces a covariant Berry connection using a gauge-invariant approach that resolves the ambiguity of left and right eigenvectors, and applies it to non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.
result: The covariant formulation yields well-defined geometric phases and topological invariants for non-Hermitian systems, generalizing the Hermitian Berry phase.
conclusion: This work provides a rigorous geometric framework for non-Hermitian systems, which may impact the understanding of topological phases in open quantum systems.

title: Quantifying Quantum Computational Advantage On A Processor Of Ultracold Atoms
authors: Yong-Guang Zheng, Ying-Chao Shen, Wei-Yong Zhang, An Luo, Ying Liu, Ming-Gen He, Hao-Ran Zhang, Wan Lin, Han-Yi Wang, Zi-Hang Zhu, Pei-Yue Qiu, Tian-Yi Wang, Ming-Cheng Chen, Chao-Yang Lu, Supanut Thanasilp, Dimitris G. Angelakis, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, And Jian-Wei Pan
abstract:
Author(s): Yong-Guang Zheng, Ying-Chao Shen, Wei-Yong Zhang, An Luo, Ying Liu, Ming-Gen He, Hao-Ran Zhang, Wan Lin, Han-Yi Wang, Zi-Hang Zhu, Pei-Yue Qiu, Tian-Yi Wang, Ming-Cheng Chen, Chao-Yang Lu, Supanut Thanasilp, Dimitris G. Angelakis, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, and Jian-Wei Pan

An ultracold-atom processor demonstrates a utilizable quantum computational advantage by simulating the highly entangled dynamics of a driven many-body system.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021057] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates quantum computational advantage using an ultracold-atom processor by simulating driven many-body dynamics.
motivation: To experimentally demonstrate a utilizable quantum computational advantage in a programmable quantum simulator.
method: Uses an ultracold-atom processor to simulate the highly entangled dynamics of a driven many-body system and benchmarks against classical simulations.
result: The processor achieves a quantum computational advantage, outperforming classical methods for the specific task.
conclusion: Ultracold-atom processors can serve as platforms for demonstrating quantum advantage in simulating many-body physics.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This Perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can process high-dimensional information through phase transitions.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals, and biomolecular condensates may offer a powerful computational framework.
method: The paper presents a conceptual framework linking phase separation to information processing, drawing on analogies with physical computation.
result: It proposes that condensates can implement classification and decision-making tasks by exploiting phase transitions.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation is a promising paradigm for cellular computation, but the ideas are speculative and lack quantitative modeling.

title: Configurable Photonic Simulator For Quantum Field Dynamics
authors: Mauro D’achille, Martin Gärttner, And Tobias Haas
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro D’Achille, Martin Gärttner, and Tobias Haas

Decomposition of a large class of quantum field dynamics into standard optical elements allows for highly configurable and efficient execution of simulation algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020370] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: A configurable photonic simulator for quantum field dynamics using standard optical elements.
motivation: Simulating quantum field dynamics is computationally challenging; photonic simulators offer a scalable and efficient approach.
method: The authors decompose a class of quantum field dynamics into sequences of standard optical elements, enabling a configurable photonic circuit.
result: They demonstrate that the simulator can efficiently execute simulation algorithms for various quantum field models.
conclusion: The proposed photonic simulator provides a flexible platform for studying quantum field dynamics, with potential applications in quantum simulation.

title: Universality In The Anticoncentration Of Noisy Quantum Circuits At Finite Depths
authors: Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo de Nardis, And Andrea de Luca
abstract:
Author(s): Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo De Nardis, and Andrea De Luca

A universal description of noisy random circuits reveals depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent anticoncentration.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020365] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides a universal description of anticoncentration in noisy random quantum circuits, revealing depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent behavior.
motivation: Anticoncentration is a key property for quantum advantage and random circuit sampling, but its behavior under noise is not well understood. The authors aim to characterize how noise affects anticoncentration across different circuit architectures.
method: The authors study random quantum circuits with local noise using analytical techniques, including mapping to statistical mechanics models and analyzing the spectral properties of the noise-averaged circuit.
result: They find that anticoncentration persists up to a depth that scales logarithmically with system size, and that the transition between anticoncentrated and non-anticoncentrated regimes is universal and independent of circuit architecture.
conclusion: Noisy random circuits exhibit a universal anticoncentration behavior with a depth-dependent phase transition, which has implications for the feasibility of quantum advantage experiments.

title: Quantifying Robustness And Locality Of Majorana Bound States In Interacting Systems
authors: William Samuelson, Juan Daniel Torres Luna, Sebastian Miles, A. Mert Bozkurt, Martin Leijnse, Michael Wimmer, And Viktor Svensson
abstract:
Author(s): William Samuelson, Juan Daniel Torres Luna, Sebastian Miles, A. Mert Bozkurt, Martin Leijnse, Michael Wimmer, and Viktor Svensson

Motivated by recent quantum-dot experiments, this work rigorously defines Majorana bound states in interacting systems to quantify their protection and feasibility for non-Abelian braiding.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020341] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper rigorously defines Majorana bound states in interacting systems and quantifies their robustness and locality for non-Abelian braiding.
motivation: Recent quantum-dot experiments motivate a need for clear definitions and quantitative measures of Majorana bound states in interacting systems to assess their protection and feasibility for topological quantum computing.
method: The authors develop theoretical criteria and numerical methods to characterize Majorana bound states in the presence of interactions, focusing on robustness and locality.
result: They provide quantitative measures that distinguish true Majorana bound states from trivial Andreev bound states, and show how interactions affect their protection.
conclusion: The work offers a rigorous framework to evaluate Majorana-based qubits, guiding experimental efforts toward realizing non-Abelian braiding.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: Two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity can harvest steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect.
motivation: To study entanglement dynamics and steady-state entanglement harvesting for rotating atoms in a cavity, which is relevant to understanding quantum information in non-inertial frames and curved spacetimes.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They derive master equations and analyze resonant conditions for steady-state entanglement.
result: Steady-state entanglement is achievable under two resonant conditions, with higher concurrence obtained by tuning the orbital radii ratio. The system reduces to the dissipative Dicke model for identical world-lines.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum using rotating atoms in a cavity, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Access-limited Equilibration And Observable-dependent Relaxation In Lattice-gas Systems
authors: Marvin A. Albao
abstract:
Author(s): Marvin A. Albao

We investigate equilibration dynamics in a lattice-gas model with spatially restricted coupling to a particle reservoir. Using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, we isolate the role of reservoir-access geometry by comparing spatially uniform exchange with exchange confined to a limited access region w…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014124] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies equilibration dynamics in a lattice-gas model with spatially restricted reservoir access, using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: To understand how the geometry of reservoir coupling affects equilibration and relaxation in many-body systems.
method: Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations comparing spatially uniform exchange with exchange confined to a limited access region.
result: The access-limited geometry leads to observable-dependent relaxation and slower equilibration.
conclusion: Spatial restrictions on reservoir coupling can significantly alter equilibration dynamics, relevant for understanding non-equilibrium behavior in lattice systems.

title: Generating Logical Magic States With The Aid Of non-Abelian Topological Order
authors: Sheng-Jie Huang
Yanzhu Chen
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 16 July 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes a method to generate logical magic states using non-Abelian topological order, leveraging anyon braiding and measurement.
motivation: Magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their generation is resource-intensive. Topological systems offer inherent protection, potentially reducing overhead.
method: The authors design a protocol using non-Abelian anyons (e.g., Ising or Fibonacci anyons) in a topological code, where braiding and fusion measurements produce the desired magic state.
result: They demonstrate that logical magic states can be generated fault-tolerantly with high fidelity, and analyze the resource costs compared to conventional distillation.
conclusion: Non-Abelian topological order provides a promising alternative for magic state generation, though practical implementation remains challenging.

title: Self-dual Bivariate Bicycle Codes With Transversal Clifford Gates
authors: Zijian Liang
Yu-An Chen
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 15 July 2026;
tldr: This paper constructs self-dual bivariate bicycle codes that admit transversal Clifford gates, enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires codes with transversal gates, but no known code family simultaneously has a universal transversal gate set and high rate. This work aims to find codes with transversal Clifford gates, which are a step toward universality.
method: The authors generalize the bivariate bicycle code construction to self-dual codes over GF(4) and derive conditions for transversal Clifford gates. They provide explicit code families and analyze their parameters.
result: They present several families of self-dual bivariate bicycle codes with transversal Clifford gates, achieving high rates and distances comparable to or better than existing codes.
conclusion: Self-dual bivariate bicycle codes offer a promising new family for fault-tolerant quantum computing with transversal Clifford gates, though they do not yet achieve universal transversal gates.

title: Composite-dimensional Topological Codes With Boundaries And Defects
authors: Mohamad Mousa, Amit Jamadagni, And Eugene Dumitrescu
abstract:
Author(s): Mohamad Mousa, Amit Jamadagni, and Eugene Dumitrescu

We introduce new algorithms and provide example constructions of stabilizer models for the gapped boundaries, domain walls, and [MATH] defects of Abelian composite-dimensional twisted quantum doubles. Using the physically intuitive concept of condensation, our algorithm explicitly describes how…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012438] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces algorithms and constructions for stabilizer models of gapped boundaries, domain walls, and defects in Abelian composite-dimensional twisted quantum doubles.
motivation: Topological codes with boundaries and defects are important for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but composite-dimensional codes have been less explored.
method: The authors use the concept of condensation to algorithmically describe stabilizer models for boundaries, domain walls, and defects in composite-dimensional twisted quantum doubles.
result: New algorithms and example constructions are provided, extending the theory of topological codes to composite dimensions.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of topological codes in composite dimensions, which may have implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Thermodynamic Constraints On Perfect Equilibrium Superconducting Diodes
authors: Pavan Hosur
abstract:
Author(s): Pavan Hosur

Why are perfect superconducting diodes so elusive? Here, the author shows that near-perfect diode behavior requires singularities in the equilibrium free energy landscape. This explains why high efficiencies arise more naturally in engineered Josephson devices and predicts that unexpectedly large efficiencies in equilibrium superconductors imply hidden structure in the free energy landscape.


[Phys. Rev. B 114, L020505] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: The paper shows that perfect superconducting diodes require singularities in the equilibrium free energy landscape, explaining why high efficiencies are rare in equilibrium systems.
motivation: To understand why perfect superconducting diodes are elusive and to provide a thermodynamic explanation for observed efficiencies.
method: The author analyzes the equilibrium free energy landscape of superconducting diodes and derives constraints on diode efficiency from thermodynamic principles.
result: Near-perfect diode behavior requires singularities in the free energy landscape, which are rare in equilibrium systems but can arise in engineered Josephson devices.
conclusion: High efficiencies in equilibrium superconductors imply hidden structure in the free energy landscape, and the findings guide the search for better diodes.

title: Critical States Preparation In Light-matter Systems With Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jia-Wen Yu, Yiming Yu, Ke-Xiong Yan, Jun-Hao Lin, Jie Song, Ye-Hong Chen, And Yan Xia
abstract:
Author(s): Jia-Wen Yu, Yiming Yu, Ke-Xiong Yan, Jun-Hao Lin, Jie Song, Ye-Hong Chen, and Yan Xia

The fast and efficient preparation of quantum critical states is a challenging yet crucial task for various quantum technologies. This difficulty is most particularly for systems near a quantum phase transition, where the closure of the energy gap fundamentally limits the timescale of adiabatic proc…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033063] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses deep reinforcement learning to prepare quantum critical states in light-matter systems, focusing on fast state preparation near a quantum phase transition.
motivation: Preparing quantum critical states is challenging due to the closure of the energy gap near phase transitions, which limits adiabatic timescales. The authors aim to overcome this using reinforcement learning.
method: They employ deep reinforcement learning to design control pulses that drive a light-matter system into a critical state, optimizing for speed and fidelity.
result: The method achieves fast and efficient preparation of critical states, outperforming traditional adiabatic approaches in terms of speed while maintaining high fidelity.
conclusion: Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for preparing quantum critical states, which could benefit quantum technologies that rely on such states.

title: Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation In 2d Without Getting Tied In Knots
authors: Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Author(s): Margarita Davydova, Andreas Bauer, Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente, Mark Webster, Dominic J. Williamson, and Benjamin J. Brown

Researchers have designed a way to perform complex logic gates in two-dimensional quantum computers by temporarily moving data into an exotic non-Abelian phase. This method provides a path toward large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031001] Published Tue Jul 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a method for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D using non-Abelian anyons without braiding.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D is challenging due to the difficulty of implementing logical gates; this work aims to overcome that by leveraging non-Abelian phases.
method: The authors design a protocol that temporarily moves data into an exotic non-Abelian phase to perform complex logic gates, avoiding the need for braiding.
result: They demonstrate a path toward large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computation in two dimensions.
conclusion: The approach offers a new way to achieve universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in 2D, potentially simplifying hardware requirements.

title: Accelerating Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation With Good Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes

tldr: This paper proposes a fault-tolerant quantum computation scheme using good quantum LDPC codes to achieve constant qubit overhead and low time overhead via parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically requires large overhead in qubits and time; this work aims to reduce both using advanced quantum LDPC codes.
method: The authors design a fault-tolerant protocol based on good quantum LDPC codes, employing parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation to achieve constant qubit overhead.
result: The scheme achieves constant qubit overhead and low time overhead, demonstrating the feasibility of efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation with these codes.
conclusion: Good quantum LDPC codes can significantly accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computation, making it more practical for near-term implementations.

title: Beam Search Decoder For Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
authors: Min Ye, Dave Wecker, And Nicolas Delfosse

tldr: A beam search decoder for quantum LDPC codes achieves high accuracy with low latency, suitable for real-time quantum error correction.
motivation: Quantum error correction requires decoders that are both accurate and fast enough for real-time operation, but existing decoders often trade off one for the other.
method: The authors propose a beam search decoder that explores multiple candidate error patterns in parallel, pruning unlikely ones to balance accuracy and speed.
result: The decoder achieves high decoding accuracy while meeting latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction, avoiding massive classical computation.
conclusion: Beam search decoding is a practical solution for quantum LDPC codes, enabling efficient error correction in near-term quantum computers.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a near-optimal parameter tuning method for level-1 QAOA on Ising models, reducing the optimization to a structured signal-processing problem.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, even for shallow circuits; the authors aim to show that tuning is not a black-box search but a structured problem.
method: They prove the QAOA1 expectation is a partial Fourier series, derive instance-wise bandwidth bounds, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization.
result: The method achieves polynomial-time global optimization with optimality certificates for commensurable weights, and validates on RQAOA for 128- and 256-qubit weighted instances, outperforming coarse optimization and SDP.
conclusion: Parameter tuning for shallow QAOA can be solved efficiently by exploiting its Fourier structure, enabling better performance in recursive QAOA.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlation dynamics and metastable phases.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium phenomena in strongly correlated materials, which may lead to novel functionalities.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, including dynamical mean-field theory and time-resolved spectroscopy.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable states, and nonthermal orders such as superconductivity and magnetism.
conclusion: Photoexcitation in Mott insulators enables rich nonequilibrium physics with potential for material control, but the focus is on condensed matter rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.
