tldr: This paper studies the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations needed to prepare graph states, establishing a combinatorial characterization and relating it to rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of graph-state preparation is important for quantum computing and communication, as graph states are a key resource.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and elementary edge-complementations.
result: They show that CZ-complexity is bounded by O(rw(G)^2) and at least Ω(rw(G)) for connected graphs, and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
conclusion: The work provides tight bounds on the complexity of graph-state preparation, but the topic is not a core focus of the user's interests.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D gauge theories.
method: They identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in a 2D spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, then use a duality transformation to map them to exact scars in the dual U(1) gauge model.
result: Exact QMBS are found in both the XY model and the dual gauge model, demonstrating a versatile construction for higher-dimensional scars.
conclusion: This work provides a new class of exact QMBS in 2D, with potential for generalization to other models.

title: Pseudo-Hermitian Magnon Dynamics
authors: Xi-Guang Wang And Jamal Berakdar
abstract: A defining quantity of a physical system is its energy which is represented by the Hamiltonian. In closed quantum mechanical or/and fully coherent wave-based systems the Hamiltonian is introduced as a Hermitian operator which ensures real energy spectrum and secures the decomposition of any state over a complete basis set that spans the space where states live. Pseudo-Hermitian, or PT symmetric, systems are a special class of non-Hermitian ones. They describe open systems but may still have real energy spectrum. The eigenmodes are however not orthogonal in general. This qualitative difference to Hermitian physics has a range of consequences for the physical behavior of the system in the steady state or when it is subjected to external perturbations. This overview reviews the recent progress in the field of pseudo-Hermitian physics as it unfolds when applied to low-energy excitations of magnetically ordered materials. The focus is mainly on long wavelength spin excitations (spin waves) with magnons being the energy quanta of these excitations. Various setups including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with different types of coupling to the environments as well as spatio-temporally engineered systems will be discussed with a focus on the particular aspects that are brought about by the pseudo-Hermiticity such as mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric assisted Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and field-induced enhanced sensitivity.
tldr: A review of pseudo-Hermitian magnon dynamics in magnetically ordered materials, focusing on non-Hermitian effects such as mode amplification and non-reciprocal propagation.
motivation: To understand how pseudo-Hermiticity (PT symmetry) modifies the behavior of magnons in various magnetic systems, potentially enabling novel functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental progress on pseudo-Hermitian magnonics, covering ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with environmental coupling.
result: Pseudo-Hermitian magnon systems exhibit unique phenomena like mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, and PT-symmetric Floquet engineering.
conclusion: Pseudo-Hermitian magnonics is a rapidly developing field with potential for novel wave-based devices, but the review does not present new results or directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and atomistic understanding.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with novel quantum materials.
conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive reference for researchers interested in Green's-function-based modeling of supercurrents in JJs.

title: Fate Of Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions From Sudden Quench To Slow Quench Limit
authors: Fuxiang Li Xiang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Previous investigations of dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT) have predominantly focused on sudden quench protocols. In this work, we systematically explore the fate of DQPT from the sudden to the slow quench regime. We establish that DQPT remains robust under slow quenching when the protocol crosses an equilibrium quantum phase transition. Conversely, we show that accidental DQPTs,which occur when the pre and post quench Hamiltonians reside in the same equilibrium phase, can be filtered out in the slow quench limit. This demonstrates that slow quenches can reveal the intrinsic connection between DQPT and equilibrium quantum phase transitions, thereby enabling DQPT to serve as a dynamical probe for identifying equilibrium quantum critical points. We illustrate these findings with examples from the XY chain, the Aubry-Andr\'e model, and the trimer Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPT) under slow quenches, showing that DQPTs robustly signal equilibrium quantum phase transitions.
motivation: Previous work focused on sudden quenches; the authors aim to understand DQPT in the slow quench limit and its connection to equilibrium phase transitions.
method: They analytically and numerically study DQPT in the XY chain, Aubry-André model, and trimer SSH model under linear quenches of varying speed.
result: DQPTs that cross an equilibrium critical point persist under slow quenches, while accidental DQPTs (within the same phase) disappear.
conclusion: Slow quenches can filter out accidental DQPTs, making DQPT a reliable probe of equilibrium quantum critical points.

title: Shielded Rl For Route-Charged Parity-Term Ordering In Qeda Phase Components
authors: Owen Friedewald, Ali Shiri Sichani, Chi-Ren Shyu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Commuting phase terms in quantum electronic design automation (QEDA) placement circuits are logically invariant under reordering, yet their routed cost varies substantially after hardware mapping, since term order affects CNOT cancellation, interaction locality, and routing pressure. We cast parity/support phase-term ordering within a QEDA phase component as a shielded reinforcement-learning problem: a feasibility shield restricts each step to unemitted terms, so every trajectory is a valid permutation by construction, and an elite (cross-entropy-method) policy is trained against a route-charged proxy combining support-transition size and heavy-hex topology-distance features. We validate by direct Qiskit routing of logically equivalent circuits to a synthetic IBM-style heavy-hex map. On 36-term parity-walk components (50 term seeds x 2 transpiler seeds, statistics at the term-seed level), the per-instance learned ordering reduces mean routed CX to 336.0, a 5.7-12.2% paired reduction over 2-opt and simulated-annealing search at equal or greater proxy budget and 22.3% over the default construction order; routed-CX and routed-depth gains are significant after Bonferroni correction. Honest transfer audits show the proxy is predictive for the parity-walk component but not for extraction-heavy or token/permutation circuits, which require architecture-aware rewards, scoping the contribution accordingly.
tldr: This paper uses reinforcement learning to optimize the ordering of commuting phase terms in QEDA circuits to reduce CNOT count and depth after routing.
motivation: Commuting phase terms in quantum circuits can be reordered without changing the logical operation, but different orderings lead to different costs after hardware mapping. The goal is to find an ordering that minimizes routed CNOT count and depth.
method: A shielded reinforcement learning approach is used, where a feasibility shield ensures only valid permutations are generated, and an elite policy is trained using a cross-entropy method with a route-charged proxy reward based on support-transition size and heavy-hex topology distance.
result: On 36-term parity-walk components, the learned ordering reduces mean routed CX to 336.0, a 5.7-12.2% improvement over 2-opt and simulated annealing, and 22.3% over default ordering. Gains are statistically significant after Bonferroni correction.
conclusion: The RL-based ordering is effective for parity-walk components but does not generalize to other circuit types, indicating the need for architecture-aware rewards.

title: Enhanced Third-Harmonic Generation In Diamond Photonic Crystal Slabs Via Doubly Resonant Quasi-Bound States In The Continuum
authors: Sangmin Ji, Satoshi Iwamoto, Hideki Gotoh
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose and numerically demonstrate doubly resonant third-harmonic generation (THG) in a diamond photonic crystal (PhC) slab, in which the fundamental harmonic (FH) and the third harmonic (TH) modes are simultaneously resonant within the same membrane. A hexagonal-lattice slab with triangular air holes is designed so that a K-point band-edge FH mode and a [MATH]-point quasi-bound-state-in-the-continuum (quasi-BIC) TH mode satisfy the frequency-tripling condition [MATH]. Modifying the hole shape from circular to equilateral triangular breaks the in-plane symmetry that otherwise forces the nonlinear coupling to vanish, thereby converting a TH mode with negligible overlap into one with finite while simultaneously reducing the required slab thickness. Guided by a closed-form expression for THG efficiency derived from coupled-mode theory, we design the unit cell and a PhC heterostructure cavity. Three-dimensional simulations of the designed cavity yield a normalized THG efficiency [MATH] under moderate quality factors, which is projected to reach ~[MATH] at the fabrication-limited quality factor (Q = 200,000). Because the operating wavelength is set by the lattice constant, this design, combined with the ultra-wide transparency window of diamond, can map a single geometry across various fabricable wavelengths, spanning from telecommunication bands to color-center-resonant visible and deep-UV outputs. These results establish a robust route toward efficient, monolithic on-chip frequency conversion in an all-diamond platform for quantum and nonlinear photonics.
tldr: This paper proposes a diamond photonic crystal slab design for enhanced third-harmonic generation using doubly resonant quasi-bound states in the continuum.
motivation: Efficient on-chip frequency conversion is needed for quantum and nonlinear photonics, especially in diamond platforms that host color centers.
method: A hexagonal-lattice diamond PhC slab with triangular air holes is designed to simultaneously resonate fundamental and third-harmonic modes via a K-point band-edge mode and a quasi-BIC mode, guided by coupled-mode theory.
result: 3D simulations yield a normalized THG efficiency of 10^-6 under moderate Q factors, projected to reach ~10^-3 at fabrication-limited Q=200,000.
conclusion: The design provides a robust route to efficient monolithic frequency conversion in diamond for quantum photonics applications.

tldr: This paper demonstrates a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for quantum chemistry on trapped ion quantum computers using matchgate shadows for tomography.
motivation: To model chemical reaction barriers accurately using near-term quantum devices by combining quantum and classical resources.
method: The workflow uses auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) with quantum tomography via matchgate shadows on trapped ion quantum computers.
result: The algorithm successfully computes reaction barrier heights with improved accuracy compared to classical methods alone.
conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical approach shows promise for practical quantum chemistry simulations on current quantum hardware.

title: Physics-inspired Transformer Quantum States Via Latent Imaginary-time Evolution
authors: Kimihiro Yamazaki, Itsushi Sakata, Takuya Konishi, And Yoshinobu Kawahara
abstract:
Author(s): Kimihiro Yamazaki, Itsushi Sakata, Takuya Konishi, and Yoshinobu Kawahara

Neural quantum states (NQS) are powerful ansätze in the variational Monte Carlo framework, yet their architectures are often treated as black boxes. We propose a physically transparent framework in which NQS are treated as neural approximations to latent imaginary-time evolution. This viewpoint sugg…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033032] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a physically transparent framework for neural quantum states by interpreting them as approximations to latent imaginary-time evolution.
motivation: Neural quantum state architectures are often treated as black boxes; the authors aim to provide a physically motivated design principle.
method: They introduce a framework where NQS are viewed as neural approximations to imaginary-time evolution, using a latent space and a variational Monte Carlo approach.
result: The framework yields competitive ground-state energies for spin models and offers interpretability through the latent dynamics.
conclusion: The approach bridges machine learning and quantum many-body physics, but the contribution is primarily computational and not directly advancing quantum information theory.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a powerful tool for analyzing high-dimensional data, but classical algorithms for computing persistence are computationally expensive. Quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and sampling techniques to compute persistent homology more efficiently than classical methods.
result: They prove a provable quantum speedup for the problem, showing that the quantum algorithm achieves exponential improvement in time complexity over the best classical algorithms.
conclusion: The result suggests that quantum computers could enable practical topological data analysis for large datasets, but the algorithm requires fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting to build zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks, with applications to NP and QMA.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on commitments not known from standard assumptions; this work aims to provide such protocols from the LWE assumption.
method: The authors extend the MPC-in-the-head technique to quantum computations, constructing three-round zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA in the common reference string model.
result: They obtain zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA secure against superposition attacks, with security based on the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem.
conclusion: This work provides the first zero-knowledge protocols for NP and QMA with superposition security from standard cryptographic assumptions, advancing quantum cryptography.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning decoding to bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code, achieving lower logical error rates than BP-OSD on small codes but not scaling well.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum LDPC codes, which are more challenging than surface codes. Machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes. The model is trained and tested on small BB codes and compared to BP-OSD and most-likely error decoders.
result: On the [72,12,6] BB code, the ML decoder achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and roughly 2 times larger than a most-likely error decoder, with consistent runtime an order-of-magnitude faster. On a larger code, error rates are worse but speed advantage remains.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: Invariant Nonequilibrium Dynamics In Gene Regulation Optimize Information Flow
authors: Benjamin Zolleralexis Bénichouthomas Gregorgašper Tkačikahttps://ror.org/0495fxg12department Of Stem Cell And Developmental Biology, CNRS UMR3738 Paris Cité, Institut Pasteur, Paris Fr-75015, Francebhttps://ror.org/03gnh5541institute Of Science And Technology Austria, Klosterneuburg At-3400, Austriachttps://ror.org/00hx57361joseph Henry Laboratories Of Physics, Lewis-Sigler Institute For Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 28, July 2026.
SignificanceEukaryotic genes switch on and off stochastically, yet cells regulate gene expression with remarkable precision by biasing the probability of switching. Recent experiments revealed a surprising and unexplained constraint: The characteristic ...
tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium dynamics in gene regulation and its optimization of information flow, using stochastic gene expression models.
motivation: Recent experiments revealed a constraint on gene switching rates; the authors aim to explain this constraint and understand how cells optimize information transmission.
method: They develop a theoretical model of stochastic gene expression with two-state promoters, analyzing the trade-off between switching rates and information flow using tools from nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
result: They find that the observed constraint maximizes the mutual information between regulatory signals and gene expression, linking it to thermodynamic efficiency.
conclusion: The work suggests that gene regulatory networks are optimized for information flow under thermodynamic constraints, bridging biology and information thermodynamics.

title: Spectral Amplification For Ground-state Energy Estimation Of Electronic Structure In First Quantization
authors: Alicja Dutkiewicz, Alec F. White, Guang Hao Low, A. Eugene Deprince III, Matthew P. Harrigan, Marika Kieferova, Ryan Babbush, Dominic W. Berry, Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate an asymptotic gate complexity improvement in first-quantized ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure Hamiltonians in a plane wave basis by employing the sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification protocol. The improvement relies on identifying a sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian which provides a lower bound certificate and low cost block encoding that leads to a provably lower quantum phase estimation gate cost. This is achieved by using a sum-of-squares operator generated by the total charge density operator resulting in a block encoding normalization improvement of [MATH] compared to prior work [MATH] where [MATH] is the number of electrons and [MATH] is the simulation grid spacing. The asymptotic reduction in block encoding normalization and similar block encoding costs to prior work is demonstrated to reduce resource estimates for materials and chemical systems by a factor of [MATH] corresponding to the lowest cost estimates for ab initio materials simulation.
tldr: This paper presents an asymptotic gate complexity improvement for ground-state energy estimation of electronic structure Hamiltonians using spectral gap amplification.
motivation: Reducing the computational cost of quantum phase estimation for electronic structure problems is crucial for practical quantum advantage in quantum chemistry.
method: The authors identify a sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian using the total charge density operator, leading to a lower block encoding normalization and improved gate complexity.
result: They achieve an asymptotic improvement in block encoding normalization by a factor of O(η^{1/3} / (k_F Δx)^{2/3}) compared to prior work, where η is the number of electrons and Δx is the grid spacing.
conclusion: This work provides the lowest cost estimates for ab initio materials simulation using first-quantized quantum algorithms.

title: Performance Model For Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows
authors: Pooja Rao, Dimitar Trenev, Jerome Gonthier, Taylor Patti, Sebastian Stern, Tyler Takeshita, Yuri Alexeev, Cedric Lin, Sam Mcardle, Justin Lietz, Katherine Klymko, Ermal Rrapaj, Norm Tubman, Krysta Svore, Peter Komar, Elica Kyoseva
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workflows are expected to underpin practical quantum computing applications, yet the quantum and HPC communities lack a shared framework for reasoning about where and when their integration requirements matter most. Such a framework must separate two distinct levels of analysis: the application level, where communication overhead affects runtime performance, and the real-time level, where it determines feasibility. To address this, we introduce a runtime model that decomposes workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs. At the application level, a communication-to-computation ratio from this decomposition quantifies whether a workflow is communication-bound or compute-bound; at the real-time level, a feasibility constraint determines whether timing requirements can be met at all, with the reaction time setting the logical clock speed of fault-tolerant computation once they are. Application of this model to representative workflows demonstrates that co-location of quantum processors with HPC infrastructure offers negligible performance benefit for compute-intensive applications today, while tight integration remains crucial for real-time tasks such as quantum error correction needed for large scale quantum computations. However, we discuss how even at the application level these assessments may shift with hardware evolution, illustrating how the model can identify specific crossover conditions, and how, under fault tolerance, the reaction time can set application-level performance.
tldr: This paper presents a runtime model for hybrid quantum-classical workflows, analyzing communication and computation costs to determine performance bottlenecks and feasibility constraints.
motivation: The quantum and HPC communities lack a shared framework to reason about integration requirements for hybrid quantum-classical workflows, which are expected to underpin practical quantum computing applications.
method: The authors decompose workflow execution into quantum compute, classical compute, and communication costs, introducing a communication-to-computation ratio for application-level analysis and a feasibility constraint for real-time level analysis.
result: The model shows that co-location of quantum processors with HPC infrastructure offers negligible benefit for compute-intensive applications today, but tight integration is crucial for real-time tasks like quantum error correction.
conclusion: The model can identify crossover conditions where hardware evolution shifts these assessments, and under fault tolerance, reaction time can set application-level performance.

title: Benchmarking Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms For Power Grid Optimization Problems
authors: Rick Mukherjee Igor Gaidai
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow Unit Commitment (AC-OPF-UC) is a difficult mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem that combines binary generator commitment decisions with nonconvex continuous AC power-flow constraints. In this work, we investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithms can improve the solution of single-period AC-OPF-UC relative to classical approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to directly evaluate quantum or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for the full AC-OPF-UC problem. We consider two candidate algorithms for improving AC-OPF-UC solution quality relative to purely classical methods on ideal quantum hardware. The first applies QAOA directly to a fully discretized formulation of the problem, with equality and inequality constraints incorporated through penalty terms and slack variables. Although conceptually straightforward, this approach requires a prohibitively large number of qubits even for small instances. The second, qubit-efficient approach encodes only the binary generator status variables on a quantum computer, while optimizing the continuous power-flow variables classically for each sampled bitstring. We benchmark this method on randomly generated AC-OPF-UC instances with 5 to 13 generators and compare it against SCIP, SMAC, and uniform random sampling. Our simulations show that the qubit-efficient hybrid method does not outperform uniform sampling. These results suggest that in order to establish potential advantage of the variational hybrid strategy considered here over the best classical algorithms, if any, much larger system sizes (25+ generators) need to be tested, which is beyond our computational capacity. Alternatively, different approaches, such as quantum versions of branch-and-bound methods, may be more promising.
tldr: This paper benchmarks hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for power grid optimization, finding no advantage over classical methods.
motivation: The AC-OPF-UC problem is a challenging mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem in power systems, and the authors explore whether quantum algorithms can improve solution quality.
method: Two hybrid quantum-classical approaches are tested: a full QAOA discretization and a qubit-efficient method that encodes only binary variables on quantum hardware while optimizing continuous variables classically.
result: The qubit-efficient hybrid method does not outperform uniform random sampling on small instances (5-13 generators), and the full QAOA requires too many qubits.
conclusion: No quantum advantage is observed; larger systems or alternative quantum approaches may be needed.

title: Basis-Independent Geometric Phase Modulation In Circularly Birefringent Plasmonic Structures
authors: Pasha Goz, Akash Das, Andre Yaroshevsky, Yuri Gorodetski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric phase in metasurfaces is conventionally realized using spatially rotated linearly birefringent meta-atoms under circularly polarized illumination. Here we demonstrate that full [MATH] geometric phase modulation can be achieved through circular birefringence and observed under linear polarization excitation. We introduce a plasmonic metasurface composed of spatially rotated chiral spiral unit cells designed to produce space-variant circular retardance. This generates a geometric phase ramp equivalent to a blazed grating, leading to [MATH] diffraction orders in momentum space. Using leakage radiation microscopy, we directly resolve these orders and show how their intensities depend upon the input linear polarization confirming the geometric origin of the phase. We theoretically analyze the phenomenon using a rotated Poincar\'{e} space and confirm our results by direct Stokes parameters measurement. These results establish basis-independent approach to geometric phase accumulation in circularly birefringent plasmonic metasurfaces.
tldr: This paper demonstrates geometric phase modulation in circularly birefringent plasmonic metasurfaces under linear polarization.
motivation: To achieve full geometric phase modulation without relying on linearly birefringent meta-atoms, enabling a basis-independent approach.
method: A plasmonic metasurface with spatially rotated chiral spiral unit cells is designed to produce space-variant circular retardance, analyzed using rotated Poincaré space and leakage radiation microscopy.
result: The metasurface generates a geometric phase ramp equivalent to a blazed grating, with diffraction orders whose intensities depend on input linear polarization, confirming geometric origin.
conclusion: This establishes a basis-independent method for geometric phase accumulation in circularly birefringent plasmonic structures.

title: Near-field Dressing Of Thermal Emission
authors: Victor Guillemot, Raphael Mol, Riccardo Messina, Valentina Krachmalnicoff, Philippe Ben-Abdallah, Wilfrid Poirier, Yannick de Wilde
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radiative heat transfer at subwavelength distances is generally understood as enhanced energy exchange mediated by photon tunnelling between neighboring bodies. While near-field interactions can dramatically increase mutual heat transfer, whether they also modify the thermal radiation emitted by the bodies themselves remains an open question. Here we experimentally show that near-field electromagnetic coupling reshapes far-field thermal emission through a distance-dependent dressed emissivity. Using a dual-probe calorimetric platform, we independently monitor the radiative balance of two borosilicate microspheres over separations ranging from 120 micrometers to a few hundred nanometers, spanning the transition from the far field to the near field. Nanowatt-resolved differential radiometry reveals asymmetric heat fluxes and a non-monotonic response of the hotter sphere, demonstrating that thermal radiation is governed not only by emitter-bath interactions but also by coupling to the surrounding photonic environment. By analyzing the total power exchanged between the coupled system and the external thermal bath, we directly extract a dressed emissivity and show that near-field interactions renormalize the far-field thermal emission of the pair through a redistribution of the electromagnetic modes available to thermal fluctuations. These observations provide direct experimental evidence that thermal emitters are dressed by their electromagnetic environment, establishing a thermal analogue of the Purcell effect.
tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates that near-field electromagnetic coupling modifies far-field thermal emission through a distance-dependent dressed emissivity.
motivation: While near-field interactions enhance mutual heat transfer, it was unclear whether they also modify the thermal radiation emitted by the bodies themselves.
method: Using a dual-probe calorimetric platform, the radiative balance of two borosilicate microspheres was monitored over separations from 120 micrometers to a few hundred nanometers, spanning far-field to near-field transition.
result: Asymmetric heat fluxes and a non-monotonic response of the hotter sphere were observed, showing that thermal radiation is governed by coupling to the surrounding photonic environment.
conclusion: Near-field interactions renormalize far-field thermal emission through redistribution of electromagnetic modes, establishing a thermal analogue of the Purcell effect.

title: Mid- And Long-wavelength Infrared Computational Ghost Spectroscopy
authors: Linzhen He, Han Wu, Wei Deng, Mingzhu She, Bo Hu, Zunwang Bo, Shensheng Han, Weili Zhang, Houkun Liang, Go\"ery Genty
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral-domain ghost imaging enables high-resolution spectroscopy with a single-pixel detector. The technique does not rely on spectrally resolved detectors, which makes it inherently robust against turbulence and particularly adapted to weak-light conditions. These features are very attractive for spectral imaging in the mid-infrared region which hosts numerous molecular absorption features but lacks highly sensitive detectors. The implementation of spectral ghost imaging in the mid-infrared has however been limited by the absence of suitable light sources and detectors capable of generating and measuring spectral fluctuations in real time. Here, we demonstrate spectral-domain computational ghost imaging in the mid-infrared based on a nonlinear frequency downconversion scheme. Pre-programmed spectral patterns imposed on broadband light at 1.5 mm using a programmable spectral filter are transferred into the mid-infrared through difference-frequency generation in a nonlinear crystal. This enables computational ghost spectroscopy with a spectral resolution of 0.62 cm-1 using a single-pixel mid-infrared detector. The method is flexible, broadly applicable and, as proof of concept, we demonstrate ghost spectroscopy in mid-wavelength infrared and long-wavelength infrared bands using the nonlinear frequency conversion in chirped-poling lithium niobate and ZnGeP2 crystals, respectively. Our approach provides a new avenue for mid-infrared spectroscopy, remote sensing and spectral imaging.
tldr: This paper demonstrates mid- and long-wavelength infrared computational ghost spectroscopy using nonlinear frequency conversion.
motivation: Mid-infrared spectroscopy is important for molecular sensing but lacks sensitive detectors; ghost spectroscopy offers a solution but requires suitable light sources and detectors.
method: Pre-programmed spectral patterns at 1.5 μm are transferred to the mid-infrared via difference-frequency generation in nonlinear crystals, enabling computational ghost spectroscopy with a single-pixel detector.
result: The method achieves a spectral resolution of 0.62 cm⁻¹ and is demonstrated in both mid- and long-wavelength infrared bands using different nonlinear crystals.
conclusion: This approach provides a new avenue for mid-infrared spectroscopy, remote sensing, and spectral imaging.

title: Grover's Algorithm For Image Edge Detection
authors: Kazuhiro Saito Pulak Ranjan Giri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grover's algorithm is one of the most significant quantum algorithms, enabling the search for a marked element in an unsorted database quadratically faster than classical search algorithms. We utilize Groves's algorithm to detect the edges of a digital image faster than any classical edge detection methods. The high success probability of our method in detecting image edges, compared to most existing quantum edge detection methods, makes it a more suitable candidate for use in the presence of noise on current quantum devices. We implemented our model for the [MATH] blocks of the image using a two-qubit Qiskit circuit with the QASM simulator and the noisy IBM Sydney(fake) device, making it suitable for most of the current NISQ devices.
tldr: This paper applies Grover's algorithm to image edge detection, achieving quadratic speedup over classical methods.
motivation: Classical edge detection methods are computationally expensive; quantum algorithms may offer speedup.
method: The authors encode image pixel values into a quantum state and use Grover's algorithm to identify edge pixels, implemented on a two-qubit Qiskit circuit.
result: The method achieves high success probability in detecting edges and is tested on both simulator and noisy IBM device.
conclusion: The proposed quantum edge detection algorithm is suitable for NISQ devices and outperforms classical methods in speed.

title: Manipulating Non-intrinsic Outputs Of A non-Hermitian Coupled System By Weak External Driving
authors: He Feng, Yi-Fan Xiang, Wei Li, Xue-Hua Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measurement provides access to exploring and understanding nature and finds widespread applications. It is generally believed that the weak external driving used in measurement introduces negligible disturbance to the intrinsic output of the probed system. Here, we reveal that dissipation in a non-Hermitian quantum coupled system induces interference between self-excitation and coupling-excitation spectral functions, giving rise to non-intrinsic outputs. These non-intrinsic outputs can be effectively manipulated by the ratio of weak external driving strengths applied to two channels, leading to significant phenomena: extreme suppression of dissipation by convergence effect of high-loss mode towards low-loss mode, and giant shift of resonant frequency instead of original spectral Rabi splitting. Crucially, we discover the Pythagorean relation linking eigenlevel splitting, spectral Rabi splitting and average total decay rate, enabling precise measurement of the eigenlevel splitting and coupling strength. Numerical simulations confirm that the interference outputs also exist in classical coupled systems. Our work provides a profound insight into measurement and non-Hermitian physics.
tldr: This paper studies non-intrinsic outputs in non-Hermitian coupled systems under weak driving, revealing interference effects and a Pythagorean relation.
motivation: To understand how weak external driving can manipulate outputs in non-Hermitian quantum systems, challenging the assumption that such driving causes negligible disturbance.
method: The authors analyze spectral functions of a non-Hermitian coupled system, deriving interference between self-excitation and coupling-excitation, and numerically simulate classical coupled systems.
result: They find that dissipation induces non-intrinsic outputs that can be manipulated by driving strength ratios, leading to extreme dissipation suppression and giant frequency shifts, and discover a Pythagorean relation linking eigenlevel splitting, spectral Rabi splitting, and average decay rate.
conclusion: The work provides insight into measurement and non-Hermitian physics, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems as defined in the research interests.

title: Scaling Regimes Of The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky Equation From The Functional Renormalization Group
authors: Liubov Gosteva, Nicol\'as Wschebor, L\'eonie Canet
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the renormalization group (RG) approach to the one-dimensional stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation and show that previous approaches based on perturbative Wilsonian RG with a sharp cutoff are not valid, even though they yield a qualitatively correct picture. The reason is that taking momentum derivatives while using the sharp cutoff is not well-defined in some cases and leads to intrinsic divergencies. This is a well-known problem of Wilsonian RG, which can be simply cured by using a smooth cutoff, and employing the functional renormalization group (FRG) framework. We establish the flow equations for the KS model within the FRG, and demonstrate that it flows to the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) fixed point at large scales. We then calculate the full two-point correlation function over a wide range of momenta and frequencies. We show that it exhibits three universal scaling regimes that we characterize: the KPZ regime (with dynamical exponent [MATH]), the Edwards-Wilkinson regime (with [MATH]) and the recently discovered inviscid regime (with [MATH]). The latter develops over an extended range of large wavenumbers and originates from the vanishing of the effective viscosity. Lastly, we investigate the large-scale behavior of the deterministic KS equation by studying the limit of vanishing noise and we determine the scales where the KPZ regime can emerge in the deterministic case.
tldr: This paper applies functional renormalization group to the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, revealing scaling regimes but with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Previous renormalization group approaches to the stochastic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation using sharp cutoff are invalid due to divergences; a smooth cutoff functional renormalization group is needed.
method: The authors employ the functional renormalization group (FRG) framework with a smooth cutoff to derive flow equations for the KS model and compute the two-point correlation function.
result: The flow converges to the KPZ fixed point at large scales, and the correlation function exhibits three universal scaling regimes: KPZ, Edwards-Wilkinson, and inviscid.
conclusion: The FRG approach resolves previous inconsistencies and provides a correct description of scaling regimes in the KS equation, including the deterministic limit.

title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network With A Modified Lorentzian Activation For Nonlocal Gradient-Flow Equations In Dynamic Density Functional Theory
authors: Dimitrios Gourzoulidis, Soumaya Elkantassi, Serafim Kalliadasis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for nonlocal partial differential equations arising in dynamic density functional theory (DDFT). Such equations are challenging for standard PINN methods because they involve nonlinearities, nonlocal interaction terms, and an underlying gradient-flow structure, often leading to slow convergence and difficult optimization. We adapt the PINN methodology to DDFT gradient-flow equations and introduce two computational components: a modified Lorentzian activation function that behaves approximately linearly for small inputs and decays toward zero as the input magnitude increases, and a precomputed discrete operator for evaluating the nonlocal convolution term efficiently during training. The method is tested on four examples in one and two space dimensions. In the first example, the exact stationary solution is known, while in the remaining cases the neural-network approximations are validated against reference solutions computed using continuous and discontinuous Galerkin finite element discretizations. Accuracy and physical consistency are assessed through [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] errors, together with mass conservation and free-energy dissipation. The results show that the proposed activation function accelerates convergence relative to the standard [MATH] function, while the overall framework maintains good agreement with the reference solutions and captures the expected gradient-flow behaviour. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed PINN framework for solving nonlocal gradient-flow equations arising in DDFT.
tldr: This paper develops a physics-informed neural network framework for solving nonlocal gradient-flow equations in dynamic density functional theory.
motivation: Nonlocal PDEs in DDFT are challenging for standard PINNs due to nonlinearities and nonlocal interactions, requiring improved convergence and accuracy.
method: The authors introduce a modified Lorentzian activation function and a precomputed discrete operator for efficient evaluation of nonlocal convolution terms during training.
result: The proposed method accelerates convergence compared to standard tanh activation and achieves good agreement with reference solutions in terms of mass conservation and free-energy dissipation.
conclusion: The PINN framework shows potential for solving nonlocal gradient-flow equations in DDFT, but the paper is focused on computational methods for classical many-body systems without quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Unified Variational Framework For Optimal Transport With Lagrangian Costs
authors: Hailiang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate optimal transport distances induced by general Lagrangian action functionals. Extending the classical Monge - Kantorovich and Benamou - Brenier theories, we derive a unified variational framework that connects several equivalent formulations of the induced transport distance, including Lagrangian, Eulerian, convex optimization, Hamilton - Jacobi dual, and Hamiltonian flow formulations. Under standard convexity assumptions on the Lagrangian, we establish the equivalence of these formulations through variational arguments and convex duality. The resulting optimality system reveals a natural Hamiltonian structure on the Wasserstein space, providing a direct link between optimal transport, Hamiltonian dynamics, and optimal control. The proposed framework extends the classical quadratic-cost theory to general Lagrangian costs and offers a unified perspective for the analysis of transport metrics generated by action functionals.
tldr: This paper develops a unified variational framework for optimal transport with general Lagrangian costs, extending classical theories.
motivation: Optimal transport with general Lagrangian costs lacks a unified framework connecting different formulations.
method: The authors derive equivalent formulations (Lagrangian, Eulerian, convex optimization, Hamilton-Jacobi dual, Hamiltonian flow) using variational arguments and convex duality.
result: The framework reveals a natural Hamiltonian structure on Wasserstein space, linking optimal transport, Hamiltonian dynamics, and optimal control.
conclusion: The work provides a unified perspective for transport metrics generated by action functionals, extending quadratic-cost theory.

title: Ptolemy's Equant Equates To A Universal Dynamical Clock Via Machine Learning
authors: Jingdong Zhang, Luan Yang, Murilo S. Baptista, Zefeng Zhang, Qunxi Zhu, Wei Lin, Celso Grebogi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Oscillatory dynamics arise ubiquitously in nonlinear systems, yet identifying a physically interpretable phase and phase dynamics in nonlinear, high-dimensional oscillations remains a central unresolved problem. Here we establish the principle of a universal dynamical clock, a physical perspective in which oscillations of arbitrary dimensionality and geometry are equivalently represented as uniform rotation through an equant-induced nonlinear viewing coordinate, inspired by Ptolemy's equant and formalised through an areal-uniformity principle reminiscent of Kepler's second law. Using a machine-learning framework, we demonstrate the existence of such an equant for a broad class of oscillatory dynamics and construct the associated dynamical clock and phase dynamics under additive forces, including noise, periodic perturbations, and coupling. Its value in uncovering new physical rules and phenomena is demonstrated by four findings: (i) collective oscillations in Escherichia coli populations obey a previously unexplained superlinear scaling law, resolving a long-standing open problem posed in 2004; (ii) the response mechanisms of engineered genetic circuits to changes in gene expression and environmental conditions; (iii) a classical-mechanics counterpart of the Berry geometric phase emerges naturally from the phase of the dynamical clock; and (iv) optimal equant non-uniformity provides a geometric early-warning signal for critical transitions and enables prediction of critical parameters. By providing operational and system-agnostic phase dynamics that can be constructed directly from data, the dynamical clock enables principled classification, comparison, and control of oscillatory systems, and offers a new route to understanding how specific dynamical regimes support distinct functional behaviours in networked systems.
tldr: The paper introduces a universal dynamical clock concept inspired by Ptolemy's equant to analyze oscillatory dynamics in nonlinear systems using machine learning.
motivation: Identifying a physically interpretable phase and phase dynamics in nonlinear, high-dimensional oscillations remains a central unresolved problem.
method: The authors establish an equant-induced nonlinear viewing coordinate and an areal-uniformity principle, then use machine learning to construct the dynamical clock from data.
result: The method reveals a superlinear scaling law in E. coli oscillations, response mechanisms in genetic circuits, a classical Berry phase analog, and an early-warning signal for critical transitions.
conclusion: The dynamical clock provides a system-agnostic framework for classifying, comparing, and controlling oscillatory systems, with applications in biology, physics, and engineering.

title: The Transition Between Synchronization And Chaos For Random Blaschke Products
authors: Renee Oldfield Cecilia Gonz\'alez-Tokman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we establish sufficient conditions for which a class of random circle maps, the so-called random Blaschke products, exhibits either synchronization or chaotic dynamics. We also establish necessary and sufficient conditions for such systems to have a unique random fixed point attractor in the unit disc. As an example, for a class of two map cocycles, we identify the random physical measures as a parameter is varied and investigate the critical value where the dynamics transitions from order to chaos.
tldr: This paper studies synchronization and chaos in random Blaschke products, a class of random circle maps.
motivation: Understanding the transition between ordered and chaotic dynamics in random dynamical systems is a fundamental problem in nonlinear dynamics.
method: The authors establish sufficient conditions for synchronization or chaos in random Blaschke products and analyze a two-map cocycle example to identify random physical measures.
result: Necessary and sufficient conditions for a unique random fixed point attractor are given, and the critical parameter value for the order-to-chaos transition is identified.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous analysis of the synchronization-chaos transition in a specific class of random circle maps.

title: Perturbation Power Selection For First-Error Delay Maximization In Enhanced Sc Decoding
authors: Zhicheng Liu, Liuquan Yao, Shuai Yuan, Zhongjun Yang, Guiying Yan, Zhiming Ma, Li Chen, Zechun Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we analyze the effect of perturbation power in delaying the first error position, i.e., the first information bit incorrectly decoded by the successive cancellation (SC) decoding. It is conducted over the finite-length perturbation-enhanced SC (PE-SC) decoding paradigm. We show that the FEP delaying probability exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the perturbation power \(\sigma_{p}^{2}\). Based on this property, an efficient perturbation power selection algorithm that maximizes the delay probability is proposed to enhance the perturbation efficiency. It results in a more efficient perturbation power selection in finite-length PE-SC decoding.
tldr: This paper proposes a perturbation power selection algorithm to delay the first error in successive cancellation decoding for polar codes.
motivation: Polar codes are a class of error-correcting codes, and improving their decoding performance is important for classical communication systems.
method: The authors analyze the non-monotonic dependence of the first-error-position (FEP) delaying probability on perturbation power in perturbation-enhanced SC decoding, and propose an algorithm to select the optimal perturbation power.
result: The proposed algorithm maximizes the delay probability, leading to more efficient perturbation-enhanced SC decoding.
conclusion: The work provides a practical improvement for polar code decoding but is purely classical coding theory without quantum information or thermodynamics connections.

title: A Zero-one Law For One-shot System Identification
authors: Nicolas Boull\'e, Diana Halikias, Samuel E. Otto, Alex Townsend
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate for any recovered model. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.
tldr: This paper proves a zero-one law for one-shot system identification of linearly parameterized analytic systems.
motivation: Determining whether a model can be uniquely identified from a single input-response experiment is a fundamental question in system identification.
method: The authors study analytic systems linearly parameterized by dictionary terms and prove that either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does.
result: A sharp zero-one law is established, reducing one-shot identification to a question about degenerate inputs and providing an a posteriori certificate.
conclusion: The result applies to dynamical systems, nonlinear PDEs, and structured matrix families, and can detect when additional probes are needed.

title: Two-Thread Coverage Mcts For Sat And Xsat

abstract: ArXiv:2607.15834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a Monte-Carlo Tree Search solver for SAT and XSAT that pairs WalkSAT-style rollouts with a two-thread symmetry-breaking initialisation: one thread starts from all-true, the other from all-false, bounding each thread's initial Hamming distance to a satisfying assignment by [MATH]. Empirically the solver closes 100/100 SATLIB graph-colouring encodings (flat200-479, sw100) in tens of milliseconds each, 20/20 planted 3-XOR-SAT at [MATH] (median 10~s), 6/6 at [MATH] (median 138~s), and one SAT Competition 2025 instance (Break-triple-04-06.xml.cnf) in 50~ms via the polarity split alone. On a full 16-round DES key-recovery encoding ([MATH], [MATH]) it drives the negative-clause count from [MATH] down to 24 (99.9% clauses satisfied) over 7 hours before hitting the S-box plateau.
tldr: This paper presents a Monte-Carlo Tree Search solver for SAT and XSAT with a two-thread symmetry-breaking initialization.
motivation: The authors aim to improve SAT and XSAT solving efficiency using a novel initialization strategy that bounds the Hamming distance to a satisfying assignment.
method: The solver pairs WalkSAT-style rollouts with two threads starting from all-true and all-false, bounding each thread's initial Hamming distance to a satisfying assignment.
result: The solver achieves fast solving times on SATLIB graph-coloring encodings, planted 3-XOR-SAT instances, and a SAT Competition 2025 instance, and reduces negative-clause count on a DES key-recovery encoding.
conclusion: The proposed method shows empirical efficiency on various SAT and XSAT problems, but its relevance to quantum information theory or the user's research directions is minimal.

title: Current Should Not Sneak: Constrained Codes For Reliable Memristor Crossbar Arrays
authors: Selahattin Kaan K{\i}rge\c{c}, Yunus Alp B{\i}y{\i}ko\u{g}lu, Ahmed Hareedy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The approach of squeezing more transistors in the same area in order to speed up computing is no longer effective. Currently, researchers and engineers are searching for novel solutions that offer faster computing. One of these solutions is to compute where you store, known as in-memory computing. Resistive random access memories (ReRAMs), which are based on memristor crossbar arrays, enable in-memory computing. Moreover, ReRAMs offer large storage capacity associated with energy efficiency. In this work, we focus on storing digital data in memristor crossbar arrays. A critical challenge here is the sneak-path problem, occurring when there is a rectangle on the array with three low and one high resistances at the corners. The electric current in this case is prone to sneaking through the low-resistance path upon reading, which results in the high resistance data becoming erroneous. In this paper, we propose effective constrained coding solutions to the sneak-path problem after finding the expected number of sneak paths over a two-dimensional array given their circumferences. In particular, we adopt a literature model where [MATH] rows on the crossbar array are read simultaneously while the others are grounded, and we design capacity-achieving non-binary constrained codes for the cases of [MATH] and [MATH]. We focus more on the sneak paths with shorter circumferences as they are more detrimental. Here, GF refers to Galois field. Our GF[MATH] codes, for [MATH], and GF[MATH] codes, for [MATH], are a class of lexicographically-ordered constrained (LOCO) codes, and we call them resistive-LOCO (RES-LOCO) codes. RES-LOCO codes operate horizontally, and we also suggest a run-length-limited scheme for coding data on the crossbar array vertically to mitigate the sneak-path problem for [MATH]. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our RES-LOCO codes for various array setups.
tldr: This paper proposes constrained codes to mitigate the sneak-path problem in memristor crossbar arrays for in-memory computing.
motivation: The sneak-path problem in ReRAMs causes read errors when a rectangle of three low and one high resistances forms, leading to erroneous data retrieval.
method: The authors design capacity-achieving non-binary constrained codes (RES-LOCO codes) for specific row-read configurations and also suggest a run-length-limited scheme for vertical coding.
result: The proposed codes effectively reduce sneak-path errors, demonstrated experimentally for various array setups.
conclusion: Constrained coding is a viable solution to the sneak-path problem, improving reliability of memristor crossbar arrays for in-memory computing.

title: Star: Astrocyte-Inspired State-Augmented Repair For Supervised Memristive Ai Hardware Systems
authors: Yusuf Ahmed Khan, Zhuangyu Han, Abhronil Sengupta
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memristive crossbar arrays have emerged as a promising platform for efficient on-chip learning, enabling local learning rules such as Equilibrium Propagation (EP) to be realized without the memory overhead of conventional backpropagation. However, as these devices age, permanent stuck-at (SA) faults accumulate at individual synaptic elements, irreversibly corrupting the stored weights and degrading model performance in ways that in-situ retraining alone cannot address. Existing mitigation strategies either rely on hardware redundancy at significant area and power cost, or require explicit fault localization that is impractical to perform continuously on-chip. This paper adopts a brain-inspired fault recovery route motivated by self-repair functionalities enabled by astrocytes -- a type of glial cell. We couple a computational neuroscience study of astrocytic neuromodulation under permanent synaptic faults with an algorithmic recovery mechanism for faulted crossbar-mapped networks. Our computational neuroscience study characterizes how astrocytes modulate surviving synapses in a bidirectional EP-specific network setting under both SA-0 and high-conductance stuck-at fault conditions, revealing that recovery operates at the neural population level. Motivated by this observation, we propose a retraining-based repair mechanism that augments EP with an additional repair nudge anchored to pre-fault activation targets of the healthy network, encouraging surviving weights to collectively reconstruct pre-fault internal representations without any information of which weights are faulty. To our knowledge, STAR is the first astrocyte-inspired repair mechanism to operate under a supervised local learning rule and to scale to convolutional networks.
tldr: This paper proposes a brain-inspired fault recovery mechanism for memristive AI hardware using astrocyte-inspired state-augmented repair.
motivation: Memristive crossbar arrays suffer from permanent stuck-at faults that degrade performance and cannot be fixed by retraining alone; existing hardware redundancy or fault localization methods are costly or impractical.
method: The authors develop a retraining-based repair mechanism called STAR that augments Equilibrium Propagation with an additional repair nudge anchored to pre-fault activation targets, without requiring knowledge of faulty weights.
result: STAR is the first astrocyte-inspired repair mechanism to operate under a supervised local learning rule and scale to convolutional networks.
conclusion: The approach offers a novel, bio-inspired solution for fault recovery in memristive AI hardware, but is focused on hardware reliability rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Do Agents Dream Of False Memories? Black-box Visual Attacks On Long-term Memory In Multimodal Ai Agents
authors: Halima Bouzidi, Mboutidem Ekemini Mkpong, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal AI agents increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory to ground generation in past visual and textual episodes. We show that unconditional trust in visual data creates a critical vulnerability. We propose Lucid, a black-box adversarial framework that compromises multimodal memory pipelines under a strictly image-bounded threat model, requiring no access to the target MLLM, target retrieval encoder, or the text channel. Lucid crafts imperceptible perturbations to enable two distinct failure modes based on the availability of historical context: (1) Memory poisoning, an in-context attack where the adversarial image replaces a benign one whose content is reinforced by prior textual context, reliably corrupting visual recall and steering the agent toward attacker-chosen narratives; (2) Memory injection, an out-of-context attack where the adversarial image replaces a benign one in a conversation turn devoid of prior textual grounding, causing the agent to generate attacker-influenced responses with no corrective signal from memory. We evaluate Lucid across various conversation domains and five black-box memory architectures, including graph-structured, LLM-summarized, and commercially deployed systems. Lucid achieves 61.6% ASR on poisoning and 58.4% ASR on injection, exposing a structural vulnerability in multimodal memory pipelines.
tldr: This paper presents a black-box adversarial attack on multimodal AI agents' long-term memory, exploiting visual data to inject false memories.
motivation: Multimodal AI agents rely on persistent long-term memory for grounding, but unconditional trust in visual data creates a vulnerability that can be exploited to manipulate agent behavior.
method: The authors propose Lucid, a black-box adversarial framework that crafts imperceptible perturbations on images to enable memory poisoning (in-context) and memory injection (out-of-context) attacks, requiring no access to the target model or retrieval encoder.
result: Lucid achieves 61.6% attack success rate on poisoning and 58.4% on injection across various conversation domains and five black-box memory architectures.
conclusion: The work exposes a structural vulnerability in multimodal memory pipelines, highlighting the need for robust defenses against adversarial visual inputs.

title: Squiro: A Framework For Security-Aware Quantum-Classical Scheduling On Kubernetes
authors: Edoardo Giusto Ignazio Pedone
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed infrastructure schedulers traditionally optimise capacity, locality, and cost, but provide limited support for security posture and emerging quantum-classical workloads. As hybrid quantum-classical computing becomes increasingly practical and post-quantum security requirements begin to affect infrastructure deployment, schedulers must jointly reason about heterogeneous compute resources, security constraints, and quantum backend characteristics. We present SQUIRO, a framework for security-aware quantum-classical scheduling based on a platform-independent Unified Scheduling Model (USM) and a six-step Scheduler Design Methodology (SDM) that together enable the derivation of concrete schedulers for Kubernetes, high-performance computing (HPC), and federated environments. The framework combines multidimensional security posture enforcement through hard feasibility constraints with residual-risk optimisation, and introduces a circuit-aware quantum backend selector that accounts for coherence margin, calibration freshness, queue pressure, and hardware capabilities through a forward-compatible colocation hierarchy. Evaluation on synthetic Kubernetes clusters shows that the security model enforces complete compliance for regulated workloads by construction, while global optimisation reduces infrastructure cost by up to 51% and energy consumption by up to 63% compared with greedy placement in underloaded scenarios, without compromising admission priorities. Additional experiments characterise the solve-time growth of the current CP-SAT formulation and show that circuit-aware backend selection systematically diverges from naive error-rate ranking under coherence- and queue-limited conditions.
tldr: A framework for security-aware scheduling of hybrid quantum-classical workloads on Kubernetes.
motivation: Existing schedulers lack support for security posture and quantum-classical workloads, motivating a unified scheduling model.
method: Proposes SQUIRO with a Unified Scheduling Model and six-step methodology, using hard constraints and residual-risk optimization, plus a circuit-aware quantum backend selector.
result: On synthetic Kubernetes clusters, the model enforces compliance, reduces infrastructure cost by up to 51% and energy by up to 63% vs greedy placement.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective security-aware scheduling for hybrid quantum-classical environments, but is focused on infrastructure rather than fundamental quantum information theory.

title: Pinching Antenna-Assisted Isac With Waveguide Mode Selection
authors: Ruotong Zhao, Yijia Zhang, Shaokang Hu, Derrick Wing Kwan Ng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15547v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional pinching antenna (PA)-assisted integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) architectures typically assume static receiver locations or predetermined receive waveguides, thereby underutilizing the inherent spatial degrees of freedom. This paper proposes a novel mode-selectable PA-assisted ISAC framework to maximize the post-combining sensing signal-to-noise ratio while satisfying multi-user quality-of-service constraints by jointly optimizing the waveguide mode selection, transmit beamforming, and transmit/receive PA positions. To tackle the resulting mixed-integer nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a low-complexity block-coordinate descent algorithm that leverages a penalty-based majorization-minimization method to achieve high-quality suboptimal solutions. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed design significantly outperforms both traditional PA and fixed-antenna benchmarks by synergistically harnessing spatial adaptability and modal reconfigurability. In particular, the mode-selectable design enables the coordinated optimization of transmit/receive operations and sensing-communication resource allocation, thereby maintaining sensing robustness under stringent communication requirements.
tldr: This paper proposes a mode-selectable pinching antenna-assisted ISAC framework for optimizing sensing and communication performance.
motivation: Conventional PA-assisted ISAC architectures underutilize spatial degrees of freedom due to static receiver locations or predetermined waveguides.
method: A mixed-integer nonconvex optimization problem is solved via a block-coordinate descent algorithm with penalty-based majorization-minimization.
result: The proposed design significantly outperforms traditional PA and fixed-antenna benchmarks in sensing SNR and communication QoS.
conclusion: Mode-selectable PA design enables coordinated optimization of transmit/receive operations and resource allocation, enhancing sensing robustness.

title: Testing Distributions Against Bounded Distinguishers
authors: Mark Bun, Rathin Desai, Renato Ferreira Pinto Jr
abstract: ArXiv:2607.15645v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motivated by the challenge of testing distributions over high-dimensional or continuous domains, we study distribution testing with respect to bounded classes of distinguishers. A representative task is to use samples from an unknown distribution [MATH] over a very large domain to decide between two cases: [MATH] for a fixed reference distribution [MATH], or there exists a distinguisher [MATH] in a bounded class [MATH] which witnesses the separation [MATH]. This is the task of identity testing with respect to fooling distance, a name inspired by the conceptual connection with pseudorandomness. (Formally, our model instantiates integral probability metrics from Boolean classes of bounded expressivity.) We show that testing with respect to fooling distance is not only a natural computational problem that admits sample-efficient algorithms even in high-dimensional settings, but also one that reveals and underlies connections between three seemingly unrelated areas of study: testable learning, verification of learning algorithms, and testing of structured distributions (whose "[MATH]-testing" model our framework extends). These connections yield new results for all of these models, including: 1. Testable proper learners using membership queries for halfspaces and decision trees. 2. A lower bound for testable PAC verification in terms of Rademacher complexity, and a distribution-free verification protocol for disjoint unions of [MATH] multidimensional rectangles. 3. Identity testers (with respect to total variation distance) for decision tree distributions and distributions with low-degree polynomial densities, over Boolean and continuous hypercube domains.
tldr: This paper studies distribution testing with respect to bounded classes of distinguishers, connecting testable learning, verification, and structured distribution testing.
motivation: Testing distributions over high-dimensional or continuous domains is challenging; the paper aims to provide sample-efficient algorithms by leveraging bounded distinguisher classes.
method: The authors introduce a framework of identity testing with respect to fooling distance, instantiated via integral probability metrics from Boolean classes of bounded expressivity.
result: They obtain testable proper learners for halfspaces and decision trees, a lower bound for testable PAC verification, and identity testers for decision tree distributions and low-degree polynomial densities.
conclusion: The framework reveals connections between testable learning, verification, and structured distribution testing, yielding new results in all these areas.

result: Discovery of unusual multiline EDSR spectra attributed to Rashba spin-orbit effective fields in quantum Hall edge channels.
conclusion: The work highlights the lasting impact of Rashba's theory on experimental semiconductor physics, but does not advance quantum information or thermodynamics.
